summary: A small, round, orange-breasted chat. Both sexes sing and defend territories through the winter, so it is one of the few European birds singing in December. In Britain it is famously tame around gardeners, but on the Continent it is a shy woodland bird.
nativeRange: Europe east to western Siberia, North Africa, Turkey, the Caucasus and northern Iran; northern birds winter around the Mediterranean and Middle East
abilities: Both males and females hold separate winter territories and sing to defend them
Sings at night under street lighting in towns
Follows large animals, and gardeners, to snatch invertebrates turned up from the soil
Migrants navigate partly with a light-dependent magnetic compass in the eye, a key study system for avian magnetoreception

animal.diet: Insects, worms, spiders; berries and seeds in winter
animal.habitat: Woodland with undergrowth, hedgerows, parks and gardens
animal.lifespan: Usually 1–2 years in the wild; a few live past 10
animal.behaviour: Territorial to the point of violence: robins attack rivals and even a tuft of red feathers placed in their territory, as David Lack showed in his 1940s experiments.
fieldMarks: Orange-red face and breast bordered with blue-grey
Plain olive-brown upperparts and whitish belly
Plump, upright stance on thin legs; large dark eye
Juveniles are speckled brown with no red breast
animal.voice: Song a wistful, liquid warble of short phrases with pauses, thinner and more melancholy in autumn; call a hard, repeated 'tic' and a thin 'tsiih'.
animal.lookalikes: Common redstart males also show orange underparts but have a black face and a constantly quivering orange tail. Juvenile robins resemble young redstarts and nightingales but lack a rufous tail.
animal.whereToSee: Almost any wooded garden, park or hedgerow in Europe; abundant wintering birds in Mediterranean olive groves and Levantine scrub.
animal.season: Resident in western Europe; summer visitor in the north and east (Apr–Sep); winter visitor to North Africa and the Middle East (Oct–Mar)

lore: A medieval legend holds that the robin's breast was scorched or bloodied while helping Christ on the cross, and Victorian postmen in red tunics were nicknamed 'robins', which is why the bird appears on so many British Christmas cards.
funFact: In 2015 a public poll organised by ornithologist David Lindo chose the robin as Britain's national bird.

summary: A plain brown skulker with one of the most celebrated voices on Earth. Males sing by day and, before they find a mate, through the night, from deep inside thickets. It winters in sub-Saharan Africa.
nativeRange: Breeds in southern and central Europe, North Africa, Turkey and the Middle East east to Central Asia (Kazakhstan, Afghanistan); winters in tropical Africa
abilities: Males command repertoires of roughly 180–260 different song types
Unpaired males sing through the night to attract migrating females; nocturnal song largely stops once they pair
Raises the volume of its song in noisy places (the Lombard effect), shown in Berlin
Migrates by night between Europe and Africa, crossing the Sahara

animal.diet: Ground invertebrates, especially beetles and ants; berries in late summer
animal.habitat: Dense deciduous thickets, coppice, scrub along rivers and woodland edges
animal.behaviour: Feeds on the ground in deep shade, hopping and pausing with its rufous tail cocked, and is far more often heard than seen.
fieldMarks: Uniform warm brown upperparts with a brighter rufous tail
Pale buffy-grey underparts with no streaks
Large dark eye with a thin pale eye-ring
Rather long-legged, robin-like posture
animal.voice: Rich, loud and varied: deep 'chook-chook' notes, liquid whistles, harsh rattles and a famous slow crescendo of pure 'piu piu piu' notes; call a soft 'hweet' and a croaking 'karrr'.
animal.lookalikes: Thrush nightingale (eastern Europe) is darker, greyer-brown with faint mottling on the breast and a less rufous tail, and its song has dry clicking phrases. Garden warbler is smaller with a short bill and no rufous tail.
animal.whereToSee: Mediterranean river valleys and scrub in Spain, Portugal, southern France and Italy; Kent and Sussex coppice in England; Turkey and the Levant in spring.
animal.season: Summer visitor Apr–Aug; most vocal late April to early June

lore: The bulbul's love for the rose (gol o bolbol) is a central image of Persian poetry from Hafez and Rumi onward, and in Greek myth the nightingale is Philomela or Procne transformed; Keats wrote his 'Ode to a Nightingale' in Hampstead in 1819.
funFact: In 1924 cellist Beatrice Harrison played in her Surrey garden while wild nightingales sang along, a performance broadcast live by the BBC as one of the first outside broadcasts.

summary: A thrush whose males are jet black with a golden-orange bill and eye-ring. Its unhurried, fluty song is one of the defining sounds of European towns at dusk. It moved from forest into cities in the 19th century, and was later introduced to Australia and New Zealand.
nativeRange: Europe, North Africa, Turkey, the Caucasus, Iran and Central Asia; introduced to Australia and New Zealand
abilities: Urban populations sing at higher pitch, start earlier in the day and are more sedentary than forest birds
Locates earthworms by sight, cocking its head before stabbing into lawns
Spreads seeds of hawthorn, ivy, yew and other berry-bearing plants
Gives distinct alarm calls for ground predators and for hawks

animal.diet: Earthworms, insects, snails; fruit and berries in autumn and winter
animal.habitat: Woodland, hedges, parks, gardens and towns
animal.behaviour: Turns over leaf litter by flicking it aside with its bill, and at dusk 'chinks' loudly while going to roost.
fieldMarks: Adult male all-black with a bright orange-yellow bill and eye-ring
Female dark brown with a faintly mottled throat and breast
Long tail, often raised on landing
First-year males have a dark bill and brownish wings
animal.voice: Song a slow, mellow, fluting warble in relaxed phrases that often trail off into squeaky twitters; alarm a frantic, rattling 'chink-chink-chink' and a thin 'tsee' for aerial predators.
animal.lookalikes: Ring ouzel males have a white crescent on the breast and pale wing panels. Common starling is smaller, short-tailed, glossy and spotted, and walks rather than hops. Females can suggest song thrushes but are much darker and not boldly spotted.
animal.whereToSee: Any European park, garden or woodland; common in Moroccan and Turkish towns and Central Asian orchards.
animal.season: Resident in most of Europe; northern and eastern birds move south and west in winter

lore: The Irish quatrain 'The Blackbird of Belfast Lough', probably composed in the ninth century and preserved in later metrical tracts, is among the best-loved early Irish nature verse; the 'four and twenty blackbirds baked in a pie' of the nursery rhyme echo real Renaissance banquet tricks.
funFact: Blackbirds introduced to Australia in the 1850s–60s became an agricultural pest and help spread invasive blackberry by eating its fruit.

summary: A brown thrush with neat arrow-shaped spots, famous for singing each phrase two to four times over. It breaks snail shells on a favourite stone, leaving a scatter of broken shells around these 'anvils'.
nativeRange: Europe east to central Siberia, Turkey, the Caucasus and northern Iran; winters around the Mediterranean, North Africa and the Middle East; introduced to New Zealand and Australia
abilities: Smashes snail shells on stone anvils, an unusual tool-like behaviour in a songbird
Repeats song phrases deliberately, building repertoires of over 100 phrases
Sometimes mimics other birds and man-made sounds within its song
Northern and eastern birds migrate at night to wintering grounds as far as Arabia and North Africa

animal.diet: Earthworms, snails, insects; berries and fallen fruit
animal.habitat: Woodland with undergrowth, hedgerows, parks and gardens; winters in olive groves and scrub
animal.behaviour: Grips a snail by the lip of its shell and beats it against a stone until it shatters.
fieldMarks: Warm brown upperparts with no markings
Buff-washed breast with neat dark arrowhead spots
Orange-buff underwing visible in flight
Smaller and shorter-tailed than mistle thrush
animal.voice: Loud, clear and inventive song in which each phrase is repeated 2–4 times ('cherry-dew, cherry-dew, cherry-dew'); call a short, thin 'tsip'.
animal.lookalikes: Mistle thrush is larger and greyer with round spots, white tail corners and white underwings, and gives a dry rattle. Redwing has a bold cream eyebrow and red flanks.
animal.whereToSee: Gardens and woods throughout Europe; huge numbers winter in Spanish and Moroccan olive groves.
animal.season: Resident in western Europe; summer visitor in the north and east; winter visitor to the Mediterranean and Middle East Oct–Mar

lore: Robert Browning wrote in 'Home-Thoughts, from Abroad' (1845): 'That's the wise thrush; he sings each song twice over', and Thomas Hardy's 'The Darkling Thrush' (1900) uses a winter thrush as a symbol of hope.
funFact: Thrushes are still trapped and eaten illegally in parts of the Mediterranean; the bird was a prized food in ancient Rome, where Varro described aviaries fattening thousands of them.

summary: A streaky brown bird of open fields that rises almost vertically into the sky, hanging there for minutes on end while pouring out an unbroken torrent of song. It has declined sharply in intensively farmed parts of Europe.
nativeRange: Europe, North Africa, Turkey and the Middle East across Central Asia and Siberia to the Pacific; introduced to New Zealand, Australia and Vancouver Island
abilities: Sings continuously in hovering flight, sometimes for over 10 minutes, at heights that make it hard to see
Nests on the open ground, needing short, sparse vegetation
Song contains hundreds of syllables and varies between local neighbourhoods
Northern populations migrate in large daytime flocks in autumn

animal.diet: Seeds and leaves in winter; insects and spiders in the breeding season
animal.habitat: Arable fields, grassland, steppe, dunes, moorland
animal.behaviour: Climbs on fluttering wings while singing, hangs high in the sky, then parachutes down in steps before dropping silently to the ground.
fieldMarks: Streaked brown upperparts and a streaked breast band
Short crest that can be raised
White outer tail feathers and a narrow white trailing edge to the wing
Stout bill and long hind claw
animal.voice: Song a long, high, rapid and unbroken warbling delivered in flight; call a liquid, rolling 'chirrup'.
animal.lookalikes: Woodlark is shorter-tailed with a bold pale eyebrow meeting on the nape and no white trailing edge, and sings a slow, descending 'lu-lu-lu'. Crested lark has a long spiky crest and no white on the tail sides. Meadow pipit is slimmer with a thinner bill.
animal.whereToSee: Arable land, downs and coastal grassland across Europe; steppes of Kazakhstan; winter fields in North Africa and the Middle East.
animal.season: Resident in western Europe; summer visitor in the north and east; song Feb–Jul

lore: Shelley's 'To a Skylark' (1820) and George Meredith's poem that inspired Vaughan Williams's 'The Lark Ascending' (1914) made it the voice of the English countryside, and 'Chakavak' is the name of a melodic section (gusheh) in the Homayun mode of Persian classical music.
funFact: Shakespeare's Juliet argues with Romeo over whether they hear the nightingale or the lark, the bird that signals dawn and his departure.

summary: The largest European tit, green and yellow with a glossy black head and a black stripe down the belly. It is one of the most studied wild birds in the world, thanks to long-running nest-box projects such as Wytham Woods near Oxford since 1947.
nativeRange: Europe, North Africa, the Middle East and Central Asia east to the Amur; eastern Asian populations are now treated as separate species
abilities: Times egg-laying to the spring peak of winter-moth caterpillars, a classic climate-change study
Learns new foraging tricks socially; traditions spread through populations in experiments
In a Hungarian cave, great tits were recorded hunting and eating hibernating pipistrelle bats
Has dozens of song variants and a large vocabulary of calls

animal.diet: Caterpillars and other insects; seeds and nuts, especially beechmast, in winter
animal.habitat: Deciduous and mixed woodland, parks, gardens, orchards
animal.behaviour: A bold visitor to feeders that forms mixed flocks with other tits in winter and nests readily in boxes.
fieldMarks: Glossy black head with bright white cheeks
Yellow underparts split by a black central stripe, broader in males
Greenish back, blue-grey wings with a white wing bar
Larger than blue tit
animal.voice: Extremely varied; the classic song is a ringing two-note 'teacher-teacher' or 'tee-cha'; also a scolding 'churr' and a ringing 'pink'.
animal.lookalikes: Coal tit is much smaller with a white nape patch and no yellow. Blue tit has a blue crown and lacks the black breast stripe. Sombre tit (Balkans, Turkey) has a dusky cap and no yellow.
animal.whereToSee: Gardens, parks and woods throughout Europe and western Asia; Wytham Woods, Oxford, is its research home.
animal.season: Resident year-round; song from late winter

lore: Its two-note song was called the 'saw-sharpener' in English country lore, and the Wytham Woods population, studied since 1947 by the Edward Grey Institute, has shaped modern ideas about natural selection in the wild.
funFact: Great tit eggs have been laid progressively earlier in the Netherlands and Britain as springs have warmed, one of the best documented biological responses to climate change.

summary: A tiny acrobatic tit with an azure cap, yellow underparts and a white face crossed by a dark eye-stripe. It is a dominant garden and woodland bird across Europe, raising some of the largest broods of any songbird.
nativeRange: Europe, Turkey, the Caucasus, northern Iran and the Middle East; the African blue tit of North Africa and the Canaries is now a separate species
abilities: Lays clutches of up to around 12 or more eggs, among the largest of any European songbird
Crown feathers reflect ultraviolet light; females favour males with brighter UV crowns
Hangs upside down to glean aphids and caterpillars from the tips of twigs
Learned to open milk-bottle tops in 20th-century Britain, a classic case of spreading animal innovation

animal.diet: Caterpillars, aphids, spiders; seeds, nuts and nectar in winter
animal.habitat: Deciduous woodland, especially oak, parks, gardens, reedbeds in winter
animal.behaviour: Raises a single large brood timed to the oak-caterpillar peak, with parents delivering hundreds of caterpillars a day.
fieldMarks: Bright blue crown, wings and tail
White cheeks with a dark line through the eye and dark collar
Yellow underparts with a small dark belly smudge
Small, short-billed and very active
animal.voice: Song a high 'tsee-tsee-tsirrrr' ending in a trill; scolds with a rapid 'chur-r-r-r'.
animal.lookalikes: Great tit is larger with a black head and a black breast stripe. Azure tit (Russia, Central Asia) is whiter below with a white crown. African blue tit of North Africa has a dark-blue cap and slate back.
animal.whereToSee: Gardens and woods across Europe, Turkey and the Caucasus; common at feeders in winter.
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: The milk-bottle raids reported by James Fisher and Robert Hinde in 1949 became a textbook example of cultural transmission in animals; the habit faded as doorstep milk deliveries declined.
funFact: Blue tits see in ultraviolet, so males and females that look identical to us are clearly different to each other.

summary: A brilliantly patterned finch with a red face, black-and-white head and broad gold wing bars, often seen in tinkling flocks on thistles. Its beauty and song made it one of the most trapped cage birds of the Mediterranean and Middle East.
nativeRange: Europe, North Africa, the Middle East and Central Asia to western Siberia and the western Himalaya; introduced to Australia, New Zealand and South America
abilities: Fine, pointed bill extracts seeds from thistles and teasels that other finches cannot reach
Males' slightly longer bills let them feed more easily on teasel heads
Light enough to cling to swaying seedheads
Some populations migrate to the Mediterranean for winter

animal.diet: Seeds of thistles, teasel, dandelion, groundsel and other plants; insects for young
animal.habitat: Open country with scattered trees, orchards, wasteland, gardens
animal.behaviour: Flocks, known as a 'charm', move together from one weedy patch to the next, constantly calling.
fieldMarks: Red face mask surrounded by white and black
Broad yellow band across black wings
Buff-brown back, white rump, black tail with white spots
Juveniles lack the red face but show the gold wing bar
animal.voice: Song a fast, liquid, tinkling twitter; flight call a cheerful 'tickelitt'.
animal.lookalikes: No adult European bird has the same face pattern. Juveniles have a plain grey-brown head but the same golden wing bar, which separates them from young serins and siskins.
animal.whereToSee: Weedy field margins, orchards and gardens across Europe; abundant in Mediterranean and Anatolian farmland in winter.
animal.season: Resident in much of its range; partial migrant from the north

lore: Renaissance painters such as Raphael ('Madonna of the Goldfinch', c. 1505) placed it in the Christ Child's hand as a symbol of the Passion, because it eats among thorns, and Carel Fabritius painted 'The Goldfinch' in 1654, the year he died.
funFact: In North Africa the hassoun is a prized competition singer, and trapping for the cage-bird trade has depleted wild populations there.

summary: One of Europe's most abundant birds: a pink-breasted, blue-capped finch with bold white wing bars. Its short song has regional dialects learned by young birds, making it a classic species for studies of how birds learn to sing.
nativeRange: Europe, western Siberia, Turkey, the Caucasus, northern Iran and western Central Asia; North African birds are now often treated as a separate species
abilities: Young males learn their songs in a sensitive period and refine them the next spring, as shown by W. H. Thorpe in the 1950s
Song shows local dialects that differ between valleys and woods
Females and young migrate further south than adult males, so northern winter flocks are largely male
Huge visible migrations pass coastal headlands in autumn

animal.diet: Seeds from the ground in winter; caterpillars and other insects in summer
animal.habitat: All kinds of woodland, hedgerows, parks, gardens and farmland
animal.behaviour: Feeds on the ground with a shuffling walk, often in mixed winter flocks with bramblings.
fieldMarks: Male: blue-grey crown and nape, pinkish-orange face and breast, chestnut back
Two bold white wing bars and white outer tail feathers in both sexes
Female olive-brown with the same wing pattern
Greenish rump
animal.voice: Song an accelerating descending rattle ending in a flourish, 'chip-chip-chip-tell-tell-cherry-erry-tissi-cheweeo'; call a sharp 'pink' and a rising 'hweet' rain call.
animal.lookalikes: Brambling has an orange breast and shoulder, and a white rump. Female house sparrow lacks the bold white wing bars. Common rosefinch males are red rather than pink-and-blue.
animal.whereToSee: Any European woodland, park or farmland; Falsterbo (Sweden) and the Curonian Spit see vast autumn passage.
animal.season: Resident in the west; summer visitor in the north and east; winter visitor to the Mediterranean and Middle East

lore: Linnaeus named it 'coelebs', meaning bachelor, because in Sweden only males stay through the winter. Belgian 'vinkenzetting' contests, in which caged males are scored on how many songs they sing in an hour, go back centuries.
funFact: Hand-reared chaffinches that never hear an adult sing develop only a simple, abnormal song, which showed that birdsong is partly learned.

summary: A tiny, round, cocked-tailed mouse of a bird with a voice out of all proportion to its size. It is one of the most widespread birds in Europe, from city gardens to remote sea cliffs.
nativeRange: Europe, North Africa, Turkey, the Middle East, Central Asia and the Himalaya to East Asia; American winter wrens are now separate species
abilities: Song is very loud for a bird weighing about 10 g
Males build several domed nests from moss and leaves, and the female chooses one to line
In hard winters dozens may pack into a single nest box or cavity to keep warm
Isolated island subspecies have evolved on St Kilda, Fair Isle and Shetland

animal.diet: Spiders and small insects gleaned from low vegetation
animal.habitat: Dense undergrowth, hedges, gardens, reedbeds, rocky coasts and moorland
animal.behaviour: Creeps mouse-like through undergrowth and log piles, then bursts out to sing from a low perch with its tail cocked.
fieldMarks: Tiny, round, warm-brown body with fine dark barring
Short tail held cocked upright
Pale eyebrow and thin, slightly curved bill
Whirring, direct flight low across gaps
animal.voice: Song an explosive, rapid outpouring of clear notes and trills lasting about five seconds; calls a hard 'tek-tek' and a dry, rattling churr.
animal.lookalikes: Dunnock is larger with a grey head and does not cock its tail. Treecreeper climbs trunks and is white below. Goldcrest is greener with a striped crown.
animal.whereToSee: Gardens, woods and hedgerows anywhere in Europe; the distinct St Kilda wren on the cliffs of Hirta.
animal.season: Resident in most of Europe; northern and eastern birds move south in winter

lore: Aesop's fable tells how the wren became 'king of the birds' by riding on the eagle's back and flying highest, and on St Stephen's Day (26 December) Irish 'wrenboys' traditionally paraded a wren from door to door.
funFact: The wren appeared on the reverse of the British farthing from 1937 until the coin was withdrawn in 1960.

summary: A slim, hawk-like grey bird whose two-note call announces spring across Eurasia. It never raises its own young: each female lays her eggs in the nests of a particular host species, often with eggs matched to the host's own.
nativeRange: Breeds across Europe, North Africa, Turkey, the Middle East and Asia to Japan; winters in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia
abilities: Female lineages (gentes) specialise on hosts such as reed warblers, meadow pipits or dunnocks, often laying mimetic eggs
A female can lay an egg in a host nest within about 10 seconds
The newly hatched chick heaves host eggs and chicks out of the nest on its back
Satellite-tagged British cuckoos fly to the Congo rainforest and cross the Sahara on non-stop flights

animal.diet: Large hairy caterpillars avoided by most birds, plus beetles and other insects
animal.habitat: Woodland edge, reedbeds, moorland, farmland with hedges, steppe
animal.lifespan: Typically a few years; the European ringing record is about 9.5 years
animal.behaviour: Females watch host nests from a perch and slip in to lay while the owners are away, often removing one host egg.
fieldMarks: Slate-grey head, back and breast; barred white belly
Long, graduated tail with white spots; pointed wings
Yellow eye-ring and feet
Rare 'hepatic' females are rufous with black bars
animal.voice: Male gives the famous far-carrying 'cuck-oo', the second note lower; the female makes a bubbling, chuckling trill.
animal.lookalikes: Eurasian sparrowhawk has broad, rounded wings and yellow eyes, and flaps and glides rather than flying with shallow, below-the-body wingbeats. Oriental cuckoo (eastern Russia) gives a hoopoe-like 'poo-poo'.
animal.whereToSee: Reedbeds, heaths and moorland across Europe in May; Wicken Fen and the Norfolk Broads in England; Turkish and Central Asian river valleys.
animal.season: Summer visitor Apr–Aug; adults leave as early as July

lore: Edward Jenner, later famous for vaccination, published in 1788 the first account of the cuckoo chick ejecting its foster siblings, an observation long doubted until photographs confirmed it in the 20th century.
funFact: The medieval English round 'Sumer is icumen in' (c. 1260), one of the oldest surviving songs in English, begins with 'Lhude sing cuccu!'

summary: A gloriously coloured aerial hunter in chestnut, gold and turquoise that catches bees and wasps on the wing. It nests colonially in tunnels dug into sandy banks and winters in Africa.
nativeRange: Breeds in southern Europe, North Africa, Turkey, the Middle East and Central Asia; winters in sub-Saharan Africa, with a small resident population in southern Africa
abilities: Removes the sting of a bee by beating and rubbing it against a perch before swallowing
Digs nest tunnels up to a metre or more long in sandbanks with its bill
Helpers, often previous offspring, assist some pairs in feeding chicks
Its range is moving north with warmer summers, with recent breeding in Germany and Britain

animal.diet: Flying insects, chiefly bees, wasps and hornets, also dragonflies and beetles
animal.habitat: Open warm country with sandy or earthen banks, river cliffs, quarries
animal.lifespan: Typically a few years; the European ringing record is 7 years
animal.behaviour: Sallies from wires and dead branches to snap up insects, then returns to bash them on the perch.
fieldMarks: Chestnut crown and back, golden-yellow shoulders and throat
Black eye mask and black necklace
Turquoise-blue underparts
Long pointed central tail feathers and long, decurved black bill
animal.voice: A liquid, rolling 'prruip' or 'krruup', given constantly by flocks overhead and often the first sign of their presence.
animal.lookalikes: Blue-cheeked bee-eater (North Africa, Middle East) is mostly green with a chestnut throat and longer streamers. European roller is stockier and blue with no long tail streamers.
animal.whereToSee: Extremadura and the Ebro valley in Spain, the Camargue, Greek and Turkish river valleys; huge passage flocks over Eilat and the Bosphorus.
animal.season: Summer visitor Apr/May–Sep; passage migrant across the Mediterranean and Middle East

lore: Aristotle wrote that beekeepers regarded the 'merops' as an enemy of their hives, and its Arabic name 'warwar' imitates its rolling call.
funFact: In 2022 a small colony bred in a quarry at Trimingham, Norfolk, and drew thousands of visitors.

summary: A tiny flash of electric blue and orange along quiet rivers. It plunges headfirst for small fish and nests at the end of a tunnel in an earth bank.
nativeRange: Europe, North Africa, the Middle East, Central Asia, South and East Asia to New Guinea and the Solomon Islands
abilities: Its blue back is structural colour produced by the nanostructure of the feathers, not pigment
Dives with eyes covered by a protective membrane and corrects for refraction when aiming
Its bill entering water with little splash inspired the redesigned nose of the 500 Series Shinkansen
Pairs may raise two or three broods a year to offset heavy winter losses

animal.diet: Small fish such as minnows and sticklebacks; aquatic insects, tadpoles
animal.habitat: Clear, slow rivers, streams, canals and lakes with earth banks; coasts in winter
animal.behaviour: Perches still over water, then plunge-dives and beats the fish against a branch before swallowing it headfirst.
fieldMarks: Brilliant cobalt-to-turquoise upperparts with a pale-blue back stripe
Orange underparts and cheek patch, white throat and neck patch
Long dagger bill; female has an orange base to the lower mandible
Stubby tail and tiny red feet
animal.voice: A shrill, piercing whistle, 'tseee' or 'chee-kee', given in low, fast flight over water.
animal.lookalikes: No other small European bird is this colour. In the Middle East, white-throated kingfisher is much larger with a red bill, and pied kingfisher is black and white and hovers.
animal.whereToSee: Lowland rivers across Europe; the Danube Delta, the Camargue, Turkish and Iraqi marshes; wintering birds on Mediterranean coasts.
animal.season: Resident in western Europe; northern and eastern birds move south in winter

lore: Greek myth turned the grieving Alcyone into a kingfisher, and the calm 'halcyon days' around the winter solstice were believed to be granted by the gods so it could nest on the sea.
funFact: Engineer Eiji Nakatsu, a birdwatcher, modelled the 500 Series Shinkansen's nose on the kingfisher's bill to reduce the loud 'tunnel boom' (pressure-wave bang) when trains left tunnels.

summary: A tall white wader with black flight feathers and a red bill, which nests on rooftops, church towers and pylons. Its soaring migrations funnel over Gibraltar, the Bosphorus and Israel in hundreds of thousands on the way to Africa.
nativeRange: Breeds in Europe, North Africa, Turkey, the Middle East and Central Asia; winters in sub-Saharan Africa, with some in South Asia and increasingly in Iberia
abilities: Soars on thermals to save energy, avoiding long sea crossings
Communicates by bill-clattering, as it is almost voiceless
Reuses enormous stick nests for decades; some nests weigh hundreds of kilograms
Many Iberian storks now winter on rubbish tips instead of crossing to Africa

animal.diet: Frogs, insects (especially locusts and grasshoppers), worms, small mammals, fish and reptiles
animal.habitat: Wet meadows, farmland, river valleys and marshes near villages
animal.behaviour: Mates greet each other at the nest by throwing back their heads and clattering their bills like castanets.
fieldMarks: White body with black flight feathers
Long red bill and red legs
Flies with neck outstretched and legs trailing
Juveniles have dull, dark-tipped bills
animal.voice: Adults are nearly silent except for loud bill-clattering; chicks make hissing and mewing sounds.
animal.lookalikes: Black stork is glossy black above with a white belly. Common crane is grey with a black-and-white head. Great white egret is all white with a yellow or dark bill and flies with its neck folded.
animal.whereToSee: Rooftop colonies in Alsace, Extremadura, Poland (Żywkowo) and Morocco; mass migration at the Strait of Gibraltar, Istanbul's Bosphorus and the Hula Valley, Israel.
animal.season: Summer visitor Feb/Mar–Aug; migration peaks in late August and in March

lore: In 1822 a stork shot in Klütz, Germany, carried a central African spear in its neck; this 'Pfeilstorch' helped prove that birds migrate rather than hibernate. Across the Islamic world storks were revered as pilgrims that travelled towards Mecca each year, and in Turkey the bird is still affectionately called 'hacı leylek', the pilgrim stork.
funFact: The European legend of storks delivering babies is linked to their return each spring and their faithful nesting on houses.

summary: A tall, grey, dagger-billed hunter that stands motionless at the water's edge for long periods before striking. It nests in noisy treetop colonies called heronries, some occupied for centuries.
nativeRange: Europe, North Africa, the Middle East, Central, South and East Asia, and sub-Saharan Africa and Madagascar
abilities: Specialised neck vertebrae let it shoot its bill forward in a lightning strike
Swallows prey as large as eels, rats and ducklings whole
Hunts by day and night, standing still for long periods
Grows powder-down feathers that crumble into a dust used to clean slime from its plumage

animal.diet: Fish, eels, frogs, small mammals, ducklings, large insects
animal.habitat: Rivers, lakes, marshes, estuaries, ditches and garden ponds
animal.lifespan: Typically about 5 years; ringed birds have exceeded 20
animal.behaviour: Begins nesting in late winter, when heronries fill with bill-clattering and harsh croaks long before the leaves appear.
fieldMarks: Grey back, whitish neck and underparts with black streaks down the front
White head with a black stripe ending in a wispy plume
Dagger-like yellow bill; bright orange in breeding adults
Flies with neck pulled in, on slow, bowed wings with black flight feathers
animal.voice: A loud, harsh 'fraank' in flight; heronries are full of clattering, croaking and bill-snapping.
animal.lookalikes: Purple heron is darker and rufous with a thin snake-like neck. Common crane flies with neck outstretched. White stork is white with a red bill.
animal.whereToSee: Almost any European wetland; large heronries in the Netherlands, the Danube Delta and English parks such as Regent's Park, London.
animal.season: Resident in western Europe; northern and eastern birds winter south to Africa

lore: The Egyptian Bennu bird, linked to the sun god and later to the Greek phoenix, is usually depicted as a grey heron, and herons were prized quarry of medieval falconers and served roast at royal feasts.
funFact: Hamlet's line 'I know a hawk from a handsaw' is often read as a corruption of 'hernshaw', an old word for heron.

summary: One of the largest owls in the world, with blazing orange eyes and tall ear tufts. A top predator of cliffs and forests, it hunts everything from voles to foxes, herons and other birds of prey.
nativeRange: Europe, Turkey, the Middle East, Central Asia and northern Asia to the Pacific; North African birds are now treated as the separate Pharaoh eagle-owl
abilities: Can kill prey as large as young roe deer and foxes
Regularly kills other raptors and owls, including buzzards and peregrines
Its deep hoot can carry several kilometres on still nights
Has recolonised cities such as Helsinki and nests on buildings and quarries

animal.diet: Mammals from voles to hares and hedgehogs, rats, birds up to heron and duck size, frogs
animal.habitat: Cliffs, rocky gorges, quarries, forests with crags, steppe ravines
animal.lifespan: Up to about 20 years in the wild; longer in captivity
animal.size: 56–75 cm; wingspan 131–188 cm; males 1.2–3.2 kg, females 1.75–4.6 kg
animal.behaviour: Hunts from a perch at dusk, gliding silently down onto prey, and often caches surplus kills at the nest.
fieldMarks: Huge, barrel-shaped tawny-brown owl
Large orange eyes and long, often raised ear tufts
Dark streaking on the breast; white throat shows when calling
Thickly feathered legs and feet
animal.voice: A deep, resonant 'oo-hu' (hence German 'Uhu'), repeated every 8–10 seconds; females higher-pitched.
animal.lookalikes: Long-eared owl is far smaller and slimmer. Pharaoh eagle-owl (North Africa, Arabia) is smaller and paler sandy-buff. Snowy owl has no ear tufts.
animal.whereToSee: Gorges and quarries of Spain, southern France, the Alps, Turkey and the Caucasus; the Sierra Morena and Monfragüe in Spain.
animal.season: Resident; most vocal in late autumn and late winter

lore: Eagle-owls were used as live decoys in German 'Hüttenjagd' hunting, where crows and raptors were shot as they mobbed the tethered owl, and the Persian name 'shah-buf' means king of owls.
funFact: A wild eagle-owl nicknamed Bubi, living at Helsinki's Olympic Stadium, briefly stopped a Euro 2008 qualifying match when it flew onto the pitch.

summary: A round-headed, dark-eyed woodland owl whose hooting is the classic night sound of European parks and woods. It is strictly territorial, with pairs occupying the same patch for life.
nativeRange: Europe, North Africa, Turkey, the Levant, northern Iran and western Central Asia; Himalayan birds are now treated as a separate species
abilities: Knows its territory so well it can hunt in near-total darkness
Hears prey moving under leaf litter and pinpoints it with asymmetrically placed ears
Fringed flight feathers make its flight almost silent
Defends its nest fiercely, striking intruders at the head

animal.diet: Woodmice, voles and shrews; also birds, frogs and earthworms
animal.habitat: Deciduous and mixed woodland, parks, large gardens and churchyards
animal.behaviour: Young owlets leave the nest before they can fly and clamber about branches as 'branchers', calling to be fed.
fieldMarks: Rounded head with no ear tufts
Large dark eyes in a pale-edged facial disc
Mottled plumage in rufous-brown or grey morphs
Stocky, broad-winged and short-tailed
animal.voice: Male gives a long, quavering 'hooo... hu-hu-hu-hooooo'; female and young give a sharp 'ke-wick'. The 'twit-twoo' of legend is a female 'ke-wick' answered by a male hoot.
animal.lookalikes: Ural owl (Scandinavia, eastern Europe) is larger and paler with a long tail and small dark eyes. Barn owl is white below with a heart-shaped face. Long-eared owl has ear tufts and orange eyes.
animal.whereToSee: Mature woods and city parks throughout Europe; often found by listening at dusk in autumn when young disperse.
animal.season: Resident; most vocal in autumn and late winter

lore: Bird photographer Eric Hosking lost his left eye to a tawny owl defending its nest in 1937 and titled his autobiography 'An Eye for a Bird'.
funFact: A tawny owl pair will often stay in one territory for life and rarely leave it, so many young starve if they fail to find a vacant patch.

summary: A sooty, sickle-winged bird that lives almost entirely in the air, feeding, drinking, mating and sleeping on the wing. Screaming parties race around old buildings on summer evenings before the birds return to Africa.
nativeRange: Breeds across Europe, North Africa, the Middle East and Central Asia to China; winters in sub-Saharan Africa
abilities: Tracked birds remained airborne for up to 10 months without landing, outside the breeding season
Sleeps in brief glides at altitude during the night
Chicks can survive several days without food in cold weather by entering torpor
Feeds on aerial plankton, gathering balls of hundreds of insects to bring to chicks

animal.diet: Flying insects and airborne spiders
animal.habitat: Open skies; nests in holes under roofs, in walls and in towers, and in old tree holes in northern forests
animal.lifespan: Often 5–10 years; ringed birds have reached about 18
animal.behaviour: Gangs of screaming swifts chase low around rooftops in the evening, then climb high into the sky to roost on the wing.
fieldMarks: Sooty brown-black all over with a small pale throat
Long, narrow, scythe-shaped wings
Short forked tail
Never perches on wires or the ground
animal.voice: A shrill, drawn-out scream, 'sreeeee', usually from groups in fast flight.
animal.lookalikes: Barn swallows and house martins have white or rufous underparts and broader wings, and perch on wires. Pallid swift (Mediterranean) is paler brown with a larger pale throat and blunter wingtips. Alpine swift is larger with a white belly.
animal.whereToSee: Over old towns and cities across Europe and western Asia from May to July; Oxford University Museum tower hosts a colony studied since 1948.
animal.season: Summer visitor late Apr–Aug; among the last to arrive and first to leave

lore: Ted Hughes wrote in 'Swifts' that 'they've made it again, which means the globe's still working', and David Lack's 'Swifts in a Tower' (1956) described the Oxford Museum colony.
funFact: Tagged by Swedish researchers in 2013–2014, some swifts stayed aloft for their entire ten-month non-breeding period.

summary: An elegant rufous raptor with a deeply forked tail that twists constantly as it steers. Almost lost from Britain by the 20th century, it has become a celebrated reintroduction success over English and Scottish farmland.
nativeRange: Europe, chiefly Germany, France and Spain, plus Britain, Switzerland and Sweden; now only a rare winter visitor to North Africa, where it formerly bred
abilities: Can stay aloft for hours with little flapping, steering with its long, forked tail
A scavenger that cleaned medieval city streets of waste
Decorates its nest with rags, plastic and other debris
Gathers in communal winter roosts of hundreds of birds

animal.diet: Carrion, small mammals, earthworms, birds, waste food
animal.habitat: Farmland and open hills with woodland for nesting
animal.behaviour: Drifts low over fields and roads searching for carrion, often in loose groups around feeding stations.
fieldMarks: Rufous body and long, deeply forked orange-red tail
Pale grey head
Long, angled wings with white patches at the base of black primaries
Constantly twisting tail in flight
animal.voice: A high, wavering, buzzard-like whistle, 'weeoo-weeoo-weeoo'.
animal.lookalikes: Black kite is darker brown with a shallower fork that looks straight-edged when spread. Common buzzard has a short, rounded tail. Marsh harrier glides on raised wings and has no forked tail.
animal.whereToSee: The Chilterns of England, Gigrin Farm in mid-Wales, Argaty in Scotland; Germany, Spain and the Swiss lowlands.
animal.season: Resident in Britain and western Europe; central and northern European birds winter in Iberia

lore: Medieval London protected kites as street scavengers; in Shakespeare's 'The Winter's Tale' Autolycus warns 'when the kite builds, look to lesser linen', because kites stole washing for their nests.
funFact: English reintroduction began in 1989 in the Chilterns, using birds mainly from Spain; the region now holds thousands.

summary: A short-winged, long-tailed hawk built for ambush, flashing along hedgerows to snatch small birds by surprise. Females are much larger than males, nearly twice their weight.
nativeRange: Europe, North Africa, the Middle East and Central Asia across Siberia to Japan; northern birds winter south to Africa and South Asia
abilities: Hunts by surprise, using hedges and buildings as cover to ambush songbirds
Females take prey up to woodpigeon size; males mostly hunt tits and finches
Long legs and toes snatch birds from the air or from inside bushes
Recovered across Europe after organochlorine pesticides such as DDT were banned

animal.diet: Almost entirely small and medium birds
animal.habitat: Woodland, farmland with hedges, towns and gardens
animal.size: 28–41 cm; wingspan 59–80 cm; males ~150 g, females ~260 g
animal.behaviour: Often seen in a brief, dashing attack on a garden bird feeder before vanishing over a hedge.
fieldMarks: Short, rounded wings and long, square-ended barred tail
Male slate-blue above with orange-barred underparts and cheeks
Female grey-brown above, finely barred grey below, with a white eyebrow
Yellow eyes and thin, long yellow legs
animal.voice: Mostly silent; a rapid, chattering 'kew-kew-kew' near the nest.
animal.lookalikes: Northern goshawk is much larger with a bulging rear body and bold white eyebrow. Common kestrel has pointed wings and hovers. Levant sparrowhawk (southeast Europe, Middle East) has dark wingtips and is pale below.
animal.whereToSee: Widespread over European farmland and gardens; huge autumn passages over Falsterbo, the Bosphorus and Batumi (Georgia).
animal.season: Resident in much of Europe; passage migrant and winter visitor in the south

lore: In medieval falconry the sparrowhawk was the hawk assigned to priests in the 'Book of St Albans' (1486), and its small male was called a 'musket', a word later given to a firearm.
funFact: Ian Newton's decades-long study in southern Scotland made the sparrowhawk one of the best-studied raptors in the world.

summary: A small falcon famous for hovering motionless over roadside verges, head perfectly still while its wings and tail work against the wind. It is the most familiar bird of prey across much of Europe.
nativeRange: Europe, Africa, the Middle East, Central Asia and Asia to China and Japan
abilities: Hovers into the wind while keeping its head almost perfectly still
Sees ultraviolet light and can detect the UV-reflective urine trails of voles
Nests in cliffs, old crow nests, buildings and nest boxes
Populations rise and fall with vole cycles

animal.diet: Voles and mice; also lizards, large insects and small birds
animal.habitat: Open country, farmland, moorland, roadsides, cities
animal.behaviour: Hangs in the air, then drops in stages before a final plunge onto prey in the grass.
fieldMarks: Male: blue-grey head and tail with a black tail band, spotted chestnut back
Female: brown above with barring, barred tail
Long, pointed wings; long tail
Black moustache mark
animal.voice: A shrill, rapid 'kee-kee-kee' near the nest.
animal.lookalikes: Lesser kestrel (Mediterranean, steppes) males have an unspotted back and grey wing panel, and it is colonial. Merlin is smaller, darker and rarely hovers. Sparrowhawk has rounded wings.
animal.whereToSee: Motorway verges and farmland across Europe; city buildings from Madrid to Istanbul.
animal.season: Resident in western and southern Europe; northern and eastern birds migrate south

lore: Gerard Manley Hopkins's 1877 sonnet 'The Windhover' celebrated its hovering, and Barry Hines's 1968 novel 'A Kestrel for a Knave', filmed as 'Kes', took its title from the hawk assigned to the lowest rank in medieval falconry.
funFact: Experiments in Finland in 1995 showed kestrels can see vole scent marks because urine and faeces reflect ultraviolet light.

summary: A huge mountain vulture that lives mostly on bone. It drops large bones from height onto rock slabs to shatter them, and paints its own white plumage rust-orange by bathing in iron-rich mud.
nativeRange: Mountains of southern Europe (Pyrenees, Alps, Corsica, Crete), North Africa, Turkey, the Caucasus, the Middle East, Central Asia, the Himalaya and Tibetan Plateau, and East and southern Africa
abilities: Bone makes up most of its diet; stomach acid with a pH near 1 dissolves bone
Drops bones from height onto rock 'ossuaries' to split them
Swallows bones as large as a lamb's femur whole
Stains its plumage orange with iron oxide-rich mud, a cosmetic behaviour

animal.diet: Bones and marrow from carcasses; occasionally tortoises and live prey
animal.habitat: High mountains with cliffs, alpine pastures and gorges
animal.lifespan: 20–30 years in the wild; over 40 in captivity
animal.behaviour: Patrols ridges on long, narrow wings and may make repeated drops of the same bone until it breaks.
fieldMarks: Very long, narrow, pointed wings and long, diamond-shaped tail
Dark slate upperparts; head and underparts creamy to rusty orange
Black mask and bristly black 'beard' below the bill
Red ring around a pale eye; juveniles all dark
animal.voice: Usually silent; occasional high whistles and shrill calls during display.
animal.lookalikes: Griffon vulture is broad-winged and short-tailed with a pale ruff. Golden eagle has a shorter, squared tail and broader wings. Juveniles can be confused with Egyptian vulture juveniles, which are much smaller.
animal.whereToSee: Ordesa and the Pyrenees, the Swiss and French Alps (reintroduced), Crete, the Caucasus, Ethiopia's Simien Mountains and the Himalaya.
animal.season: Resident; nests in midwinter

lore: The Persian Homa (Huma), a bird whose shadow bestowed kingship, has long been associated with the bearded vulture, and Pliny repeats the legend that the playwright Aeschylus was killed by a tortoise dropped by an eagle onto his bald head.
funFact: It was exterminated from the Alps by the early 20th century; reintroduction since 1986 has re-established a wild breeding population there.

summary: One of the heaviest flying birds on Earth. Males transform themselves in spring into billowing white 'foam baths' of feathers to impress females on open steppe and farmland. Most of the world population now lives in Spain.
nativeRange: Iberia, central Europe (Hungary, Austria, Germany), Morocco, Turkey, Russia, Kazakhstan, Central Asia and Mongolia to China; reintroduced to England
abilities: Males weigh up to about 16 kg, contesting the title of heaviest flying animal
Displaying males turn wings and tail inside out to become a mass of white plumes
Males grow long white whisker feathers in the breeding season
Lek-like display grounds are used for generations

animal.diet: Plant shoots, leaves, seeds, legumes; insects such as beetles and grasshoppers, especially for chicks
animal.habitat: Open steppe, extensive cereal farmland and pasture
animal.lifespan: Typically about 10 years; some exceed 15, with a maximum recorded age of 28
animal.size: Males 90–105 cm, 5.8–16 kg; females 75–85 cm, 3.3–5.3 kg; wingspan 1.9–2.6 m
animal.behaviour: Males gather on traditional display grounds in spring, where females visit to choose a mate.
fieldMarks: Very large, stately, goose-sized ground bird with long neck and legs
Upperparts golden-buff barred with black
Grey head and neck; males with chestnut breast band and white whiskers
Huge white wing panels in flight
animal.voice: Generally silent; a low barking or grunting at close quarters.
animal.lookalikes: Little bustard is much smaller (pheasant-sized) with a black-and-white neck in males. Asian houbara is sandy with a black neck plume. Female great bustard is far smaller than the male and can be mistaken for a goose at distance.
animal.whereToSee: Villafáfila and Extremadura in Spain, Castro Verde in Portugal, Hungary's Dévaványa, Salisbury Plain in England (reintroduced).
animal.season: Resident in Iberia; partially migratory in Russia and Central Asia; display Mar–Apr

lore: Bustards were exterminated in Britain by the 1830s; the bird still appears on Wiltshire's county emblem, and a reintroduction using chicks from Russia and Spain began on Salisbury Plain in 2004.
funFact: Its Latin name 'tarda' means 'slow', but despite its weight it is a strong flier.

summary: A sandy, cryptic bustard of deserts and semi-deserts that is the classic quarry of Arab falconry. Hunting and trapping along its migration routes have driven it into decline despite large captive-breeding programmes.
nativeRange: Breeds from Sinai, the Middle East and Iran across Central Asia to Mongolia and China; winters in the Arabian Peninsula, Iran, Pakistan and northwestern India
abilities: Plumage blends almost perfectly with sand and gravel desert
Can obtain water largely from food in arid habitats
Migrates thousands of kilometres between Central Asian breeding grounds and South Asian or Arabian wintering grounds
Squirts a jet of faeces at attacking falcons as a defence

animal.diet: Shoots, seeds and fruits of desert plants; beetles, locusts and small reptiles
animal.habitat: Flat or rolling semi-desert with sparse shrubs
animal.behaviour: Displaying males raise their white neck plumes over their heads and run in zigzags, a display visible from far across the desert.
fieldMarks: Sandy buff upperparts finely vermiculated with black
Black stripe running down each side of the neck into a white ruff
Short crest of white and black feathers
Bold black-and-white wing pattern in flight
animal.voice: Mostly silent; a low booming during display.
animal.lookalikes: African houbara (Chlamydotis undulata) of North Africa is very similar but has an all-white crest; ranges barely overlap. Great bustard is much larger, grey-headed and lacks the black neck stripe.
animal.whereToSee: Kyzylkum Desert in Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan in spring; Cholistan and Balochistan (Pakistan) and the UAE in winter.
animal.season: Summer visitor to Central Asia Mar–Oct; winter visitor to Arabia and South Asia

lore: Hunting houbara with sakers and peregrines is a centuries-old Bedouin tradition, and special permits for Gulf rulers to hunt it in Pakistan have been the subject of court challenges in Pakistan's Supreme Court.
funFact: Captive-breeding centres in the UAE, Saudi Arabia and Morocco release large numbers of captive-bred houbara to support wild populations and falconry.

summary: A crested, iridescent plover of fields and wet meadows, named for the 'lapping' sound of its floppy, rounded wings in its tumbling display flight. Breeding numbers have fallen sharply with farming changes across Europe.
nativeRange: Breeds across temperate Europe and Asia from Ireland to the Pacific; winters in western Europe, North Africa, the Middle East, South Asia and China
abilities: Tumbling display flight with wing-throbbing sound and wild calls
Parents mob crows and foxes and perform distraction displays to lure predators away
Chicks feed themselves within hours of hatching
Cold-weather movements can shift huge flocks hundreds of kilometres in a day

animal.diet: Earthworms, beetles, leatherjackets and other soil invertebrates
animal.habitat: Wet grassland, spring-sown fields, marshes; mudflats and pastures in winter
animal.behaviour: Feeds with a 'stop-run-tilt' action and patters its feet on the ground to bring worms up.
fieldMarks: Long, wispy black crest
Dark green upperparts with purple and bronze gloss
Black breast band, white belly, orange undertail
Broad, rounded black-and-white wings in flight
animal.voice: A plaintive, wheezy 'pee-wit' and wild, twisting display song 'pee-wit wit-wit eeze'.
animal.lookalikes: No other European bird has the long crest. Sociable lapwing is sandy with a dark cap and white eyebrow. Golden plover, often in mixed winter flocks, has pointed wings and spangled golden upperparts.
animal.whereToSee: Wet meadows of the Netherlands, Somerset Levels and RSPB reserves in England; huge winter flocks across western Europe and the Nile Delta.
animal.season: Resident or partial migrant in western Europe; summer visitor further east; winter visitor to the Mediterranean and Middle East

lore: In Friesland the first lapwing egg of spring is traditionally presented to the province's King's Commissioner; since collecting was banned, the hunt continues as a search without taking.
funFact: Its English name comes from Old English 'hleapewince', referring to its leaping, wavering flight.

summary: Europe's largest wader, with a very long, down-curved bill and a bubbling, haunting call that carries over moors and estuaries. It has declined steeply in Britain and Ireland, which hold a large share of the world's breeding birds.
nativeRange: Breeds from Britain and Ireland across northern and central Europe and Central Asia to Siberia; winters on coasts of western Europe, Africa, the Middle East and South Asia
abilities: Probes deep into mud for lugworms and ragworms with a bill up to about 15 cm long in females
The bill tip is flexible and sensitive, letting it feel for prey underground
Females have longer bills than males, so the sexes feed differently
Gathers in large flocks at estuary high-tide roosts

animal.diet: Worms, crabs, molluscs and insects; leatherjackets and earthworms inland
animal.habitat: Moorland, rough pasture and wet meadows for breeding; estuaries and mudflats in winter
animal.behaviour: On breeding grounds it rises on fluttering wings and glides down giving its bubbling song.
fieldMarks: Very long, down-curved bill
Grey-brown streaked plumage
White wedge up the rump and back in flight
Large size; long, blue-grey legs
animal.voice: A rising, mournful 'cur-lee' and a long, accelerating bubbling trill in display.
animal.lookalikes: Whimbrel is smaller with a shorter bill, a striped crown and a rapid seven-note 'tititititi' call. Bar-tailed godwit has a slightly upturned bill.
animal.whereToSee: Pennine and Scottish moors in spring; the Wash, Morecambe Bay, the Wadden Sea and Banc d'Arguin (Mauritania) in winter.
animal.season: Present on coasts all year; on moorland breeding grounds Mar–Jul

lore: W. B. Yeats used its cry as an image of grief in 'He Reproves the Curlew' (1899), and Benjamin Britten's church parable 'Curlew River' (1964) takes its title from the bird.
funFact: Its smaller relative the slender-billed curlew was last confirmed in Morocco in 1995, and a 2024 study concluded it is very likely extinct.

summary: A tall, grey crane with a black-and-white head and a bushy tail-bustle, whose trumpeting flocks pass over Europe in spring and autumn. Paired birds perform elaborate leaping, bowing dances.
nativeRange: Breeds from Scandinavia and Germany across northern Europe and Asia to eastern Siberia; winters in Iberia, France, North Africa, the Middle East, India and China
abilities: A long, coiled windpipe within the breastbone amplifies its far-carrying trumpet calls
Pairs duet in synchronised 'unison calls'
Migrates in V-formations, with major stopovers used by tens of thousands
Stains its plumage brown with mud when nesting, for camouflage

animal.diet: Grain, roots, acorns, shoots; insects, frogs and small animals in summer
animal.habitat: Bogs, forest swamps and marshes for breeding; open farmland and wetlands in winter
animal.behaviour: Dancing cranes bow, leap into the air with wings spread and toss sticks, at any time of year.
fieldMarks: Tall and grey with long black legs
Black head and neck with a white stripe behind the eye; red crown patch
Drooping tail-bustle of curved inner wing feathers
Flies with neck outstretched
animal.voice: A loud, rolling, bugling 'krroo-krroo', audible from kilometres away.
animal.lookalikes: Grey heron flies with neck folded and lacks the black head. Demoiselle crane is smaller with black breast plumes and white ear tufts. White stork is white with a red bill.
animal.whereToSee: Lake Hornborgasjön (Sweden) in April, Rügen-Bock (Germany) and Lac du Der (France) in autumn, Gallocanta (Spain), Hula Valley (Israel) in winter; the Norfolk Broads and Somerset Levels in England.
animal.season: Summer visitor to northern Europe Mar–Oct; passage migrant; winter visitor to the Mediterranean and Middle East

lore: In Greek legend the cranes of Ibycus witnessed the poet's murder and revealed his killers, and Persian poetry uses the call of the 'kulang' and 'dorna' as an image of exile and longing.
funFact: Cranes returned to England's Norfolk Broads in 1979 and first bred there in 1981, around 400 years after they were lost as a breeding bird.

summary: A brilliant yellow-and-black bird that is surprisingly hard to see, hidden in the leafy canopy of poplars and oaks. Its loud, fluting whistle betrays it long before a glimpse of gold.
nativeRange: Breeds across Europe, northwest Africa, Turkey, the Middle East and Central Asia to western Siberia; winters in sub-Saharan Africa
abilities: Builds a hammock-like nest slung between the forks of a high branch
Its bright yellow plumage is remarkably well hidden among sunlit leaves
Migrates by night to wintering grounds in tropical Africa
Can handle hairy caterpillars that many birds avoid

animal.diet: Insects and caterpillars; fruit, cherries and berries in late summer
animal.habitat: Tall deciduous woods, riverine poplar groves, orchards and parks
animal.behaviour: Moves through the canopy in swooping, undulating flights between trees, rarely coming low.
fieldMarks: Male bright golden-yellow with black wings and black centre to the tail
Pink-red bill and black lores
Female and young greenish-yellow with streaked whitish underparts
Thrush-sized with a woodpecker-like undulating flight
animal.voice: A rich, fluting whistle often rendered 'weela-weeoo' or 'dee-dlee-o'; also a harsh, cat-like 'kweeaah'.
animal.lookalikes: Female resembles green woodpecker in flight, but lacks red on the head. Indian golden oriole (South Asia) has black extending behind the eye. Yellow wagtail and yellowhammer are smaller and ground-living.
animal.whereToSee: Poplar plantations and riverine woods in Spain, France, the Danube Delta, Turkey and the Central Asian river valleys; a rare spring migrant to eastern England, where it last bred in 2009.
animal.season: Summer visitor May–Aug

lore: Pliny the Elder reported the belief that a jaundice sufferer who looked at the 'icterus', a yellow bird usually identified as the oriole, would be cured while the bird died.
funFact: The German name 'Pirol' and Dutch 'wielewaal' are both imitations of its whistled song.

summary: The largest seabird of the North Atlantic, a dazzling white diver with black wingtips and a buttery head. It plunges from height into the sea for fish and breeds in vast, crowded colonies on cliffs and stacks.
nativeRange: North Atlantic: breeds in Britain, Ireland, Iceland, Norway, France, Canada; winters south to West Africa and the Gulf of Mexico, and into the Mediterranean
abilities: Plunge-dives from up to about 30 m, hitting the water at high speed
Air sacs under the skin of the face and chest cushion the impact
Has no external nostrils, which stops water entering on impact
Forward-facing eyes give binocular vision for judging the strike

animal.diet: Shoaling fish such as mackerel, herring and sandeels
animal.habitat: Continental-shelf seas; breeds on islands and sea cliffs
animal.behaviour: Pairs greet each other at the nest by 'sky-pointing' and fencing with their bills, and defend a tiny nest site fiercely.
fieldMarks: Large, cigar-shaped white seabird with long, narrow wings
Black wingtips
Yellow-buff head and nape in adults
Dagger bill; juveniles dark brown with white speckles, whitening over four or five years
animal.voice: Silent at sea; colonies resound with harsh, grating 'urrah' calls.
animal.lookalikes: Great black-backed and other large gulls have rounded wings and lack the pointed tail. Cory's shearwater is brown above. Distant juveniles can suggest brown boobies, which are only rare vagrants in European waters.
animal.whereToSee: Bass Rock (Scotland), Bempton Cliffs (England), Grassholm (Wales), St Kilda, Little Skellig (Ireland), Bonaventure Island (Quebec); offshore passage along Atlantic coasts.
animal.season: At colonies Jan–Oct; offshore passage in autumn; winter at sea

lore: Its scientific name honours Scotland's Bass Rock, one of the largest northern gannet colonies in the world, and men from Ness on Lewis have for centuries made a licensed 'guga hunt' for young gannets on the rock of Sula Sgeir, though it has been suspended or refused in several years since the 2022 bird-flu outbreak.
funFact: After the 2022 avian influenza outbreak, many surviving gannets on Bass Rock had irises turned from pale blue to black.

summary: The world's largest grouse, a turkey-sized black cock of old pine forests that fans its tail and clicks, pops and gurgles at dawn displays. It survives a whole winter largely on pine needles.
nativeRange: Boreal and mountain conifer forests from Scotland, Scandinavia, the Alps, Pyrenees and Cantabrians across Russia to central Siberia
abilities: Survives winter mainly on pine needles, digested with the help of long caeca
Males are roughly twice the size of females
Displaying males are so absorbed in their song that they briefly cannot hear, giving the Russian name 'glukhar' (deaf one)
Aggressive males in display sometimes attack people and vehicles

animal.diet: Pine needles in winter; bilberry leaves and berries, buds, shoots, seeds; insects for chicks
animal.habitat: Old, open conifer forests with a rich bilberry understorey
animal.size: Males 74–90 cm, around 4 kg; females 54–63 cm, around 1.8 kg
animal.behaviour: Males gather at traditional leks at dawn in spring, strutting with fanned tails and raised beards.
fieldMarks: Male huge and dark slate-grey with a glossy green breast
Fanned, rounded black tail and shaggy throat 'beard'
Ivory bill and red wattle above the eye
Female much smaller, barred brown with a rufous breast patch
animal.voice: Male display song is a sequence of accelerating clicks ending in a 'pop' like a cork and a wheezing, scraping phrase.
animal.lookalikes: Black grouse is smaller with a lyre-shaped tail and white undertail. Female capercaillie can be confused with female black grouse but is larger with a plain orange-rufous breast and rounded tail.
animal.whereToSee: Abernethy Forest and Strathspey (Scotland), Finnish and Swedish taiga, the Bavarian Forest, the Alps and the Pyrenees; leks must be watched only on guided visits.
animal.season: Resident; leks Apr–May

lore: Hunted out of Scotland by about 1785, it was reintroduced from Sweden to Taymouth Castle in Perthshire in 1837; the Gaelic name means 'horse of the woods'.
funFact: The Scottish population has fallen to a few hundred birds and is now largely confined to Strathspey.

summary: A glossy blue-black grouse with a lyre-shaped tail, white undertail puff and red eyebrows. Males gather at dawn leks to bubble and hiss in one of Europe's great wildlife spectacles.
nativeRange: Britain, Scandinavia, the Alps, eastern Europe, Russia and Siberia to northern Mongolia and northeastern China
abilities: Males display communally at leks, with dominant central males getting most matings
Burrows into snow to roost during cold nights
Feeds on birch buds and catkins through hard winters
Chicks depend heavily on insects, especially sawfly larvae

animal.diet: Birch buds and catkins, heather, bilberry, conifer needles; insects for chicks
animal.habitat: Moorland edge, open woodland, forest clearings and bogs
animal.size: Males 49–58 cm, ~1.2 kg; females 40–45 cm, ~0.9 kg
animal.behaviour: At the lek, males crouch with fanned white undertail and spread wings, rushing at rivals and jumping into the air.
fieldMarks: Male glossy blue-black with a lyre-shaped forked tail
White wing bar and white undertail fluffed in display
Red wattles above the eyes
Female ('greyhen') grey-brown, barred, with a slightly forked tail and thin white wing bar
animal.voice: Male makes a dove-like bubbling 'rookooing' and an explosive sneezing 'tchu-shweee'.
animal.lookalikes: Capercaillie is much larger with a rounded tail. Female resembles female red grouse but is larger and greyer with a forked tail. Caucasian grouse (Caucasus) has a longer, more deeply forked tail without white undertail.
animal.whereToSee: Leks in Scottish Highland glens and the Pennines, Finnish and Swedish bogs, the Alps above the treeline.
animal.season: Resident; leks Mar–May at dawn

lore: The curved tail feather of the black cock (Spielhahnfeder) is the traditional hat ornament of Alpine hunters in Bavaria and Tyrol.
funFact: Black grouse occasionally hybridise with capercaillie, producing a bird that German hunters call the 'Rackelhahn'.

summary: A small grey cliff-dweller that flicks open its wings to flash crimson patches like a butterfly while it creeps up sheer rock faces. It is the only member of its family and one of the most sought-after birds in Europe.
nativeRange: High mountains from the Cantabrians, Pyrenees and Alps through the Balkans, Turkey, the Caucasus and Iran to Central Asia, the Himalaya and western China
abilities: Climbs vertical rock faces using long claws and constant wing-flicking
Probes cracks for spiders and insects with a long, fine, down-curved bill
Descends to lower cliffs, quarries and even old buildings in winter
Sole living species of the family Tichodromidae

animal.diet: Spiders, insects and their larvae from rock crevices
animal.habitat: Damp cliffs and gorges, often near waterfalls, from about 1,000 m to over 3,000 m
animal.behaviour: Moves up a cliff in jerky hops with wings half-open, then drops back down in fluttering flight to start again.
fieldMarks: Ash-grey body and short black tail
Broad, rounded wings with large crimson patches and white spots
Long, thin, down-curved black bill
Breeding male has a black throat; white in winter
animal.voice: Song a series of thin, rising whistles, 'tu-tu-tueee'; mostly silent otherwise.
animal.lookalikes: No other bird looks the same. In flight at distance it can suggest a large butterfly or a hoopoe, but the hoopoe is much larger and has a crest.
animal.whereToSee: Gorges in the Pyrenees (Ordesa), Swiss and Italian Alps, Picos de Europa, the Taurus Mountains and the Caucasus; winter at castles and quarries in southern Europe.
animal.season: Resident at altitude; moves lower in winter (Oct–Mar)

lore: Its scientific name, coined by Johann Illiger in 1811, combines Greek 'teichos' (wall) and 'dromos' (runner), and Linnaeus had placed it among the treecreepers as Certhia muraria.
funFact: Unlike treecreepers and nuthatches, it does not use its tail as a prop when climbing.

summary: A colourful, shy woodland crow, pinkish-brown with a white rump and a dazzling blue-barred wing patch. Each autumn it buries thousands of acorns, and the ones it forgets grow into new oak woods.
nativeRange: Europe, North Africa, Turkey, the Middle East, the Caucasus and Central Asia, across Asia to Japan and Southeast Asia
abilities: A single jay may cache several thousand acorns in an autumn
Remembers cache locations months later, even under snow
Its forgotten caches are a major means by which oaks spread uphill and into open land
Skilled mimic of other birds, especially buzzards and owls

animal.diet: Acorns, beechmast and other seeds; insects, eggs and nestling birds in summer
animal.habitat: Oak and mixed woodland, parks, large gardens
animal.behaviour: Carries several acorns at once in its throat pouch and bill, pushing each into the ground and covering it with leaves.
fieldMarks: Pinkish-buff body with a bright white rump contrasting with a black tail
Blue-and-black barred patch on the wing
Black moustache stripe and streaked crest
Floppy, rounded wings in flight
animal.voice: A harsh, tearing screech, 'skaaak', the alarm call of the woods; also soft mewing and mimicry.
animal.lookalikes: No other European bird combines the white rump and blue wing patch. Hoopoe also shows a black-and-white pattern in flight but has a long, curved bill and fan crest. Middle Eastern races have a black crown.
animal.whereToSee: Oak woods throughout Europe, most visible in September–October when carrying acorns.
animal.season: Resident; occasional large irruptions in autumn when acorn crops fail

lore: The specific name 'glandarius' means 'of acorns', and the blue wing feathers were sold to Victorian milliners and fly-tyers; jays were persecuted by gamekeepers as egg thieves.
funFact: Studies at Cambridge showed male jays choose food gifts for their mates based on what the female has recently been eating, suggesting they track another bird's desires.

summary: A bold, long-tailed black-and-white crow with iridescent blue and green gloss. Clever and adaptable, it is a familiar bird of farmland and towns, surrounded by centuries of superstition.
nativeRange: Europe, Turkey, the Middle East and Central Asia to Siberia; birds of North Africa, southwest Arabia and East Asia are now often treated as separate species
abilities: In 2008 it became the first non-mammal shown to recognise itself in a mirror
Builds a large domed nest of sticks with a mud-lined cup
Caches food and recaches it if watched by other magpies
Thrives in cities and farmland across much of Eurasia

animal.diet: Omnivorous: insects, grain, fruit, carrion, small animals, eggs and nestlings
animal.habitat: Open country with scattered trees and hedges, parks, suburbs
animal.size: 40–51 cm including tail; wingspan 52–60 cm; 160–250 g
animal.behaviour: Gathers in noisy groups ('parliaments') in late winter and mobs cats, foxes and owls.
fieldMarks: Black head, breast and back with white belly and shoulders
Very long, graduated tail glossed green and purple
Wings glossed blue with white primaries flashing in flight
Strong black bill and legs
animal.voice: A loud, rapid, rattling chatter, 'chak-chak-chak-chak'.
animal.lookalikes: No other European bird has the same shape and pattern. Iberian (azure-winged) magpie is smaller with a black cap and pale-blue wings and tail. Maghreb magpie (North Africa) has bare blue skin behind the eye.
animal.whereToSee: Farmland, parks and suburbs across Europe, Turkey and Central Asia.
animal.season: Resident

lore: The British counting rhyme 'One for sorrow, two for joy' is first recorded in the 18th century, and Rossini's opera 'La gazza ladra' (The Thieving Magpie, 1817) cemented its reputation as a thief.
funFact: A 2014 Exeter study found that wild magpies are actually wary of shiny objects, contradicting the thieving-magpie myth.

summary: A large, powerful falcon of steppe and semi-desert, prized for millennia by falconers from Arabia to Mongolia. Electrocution on power lines and capture for the falconry trade have pushed it to Endangered.
nativeRange: Breeds from central Europe (Hungary, Slovakia, Austria) through Ukraine, Turkey, Russia, Kazakhstan and Central Asia to Mongolia and China; winters south to the Middle East, northeast Africa and South Asia
abilities: Hunts ground squirrels (sousliks) close to the ground with fast, low pursuit flights
Can take prey as large as houbara bustards when trained
Uses nests built by other birds, including on power pylons
Readily breeds in artificial nest boxes on pylons, a key conservation tool in Hungary and Mongolia

animal.diet: Ground squirrels, voles, pikas, hamsters; birds such as pigeons and partridges
animal.habitat: Open steppe, wooded steppe, semi-desert, farmland with pylons
animal.lifespan: Typically under 10 years in the wild; 20+ in captivity
animal.size: 47–57 cm; wingspan 97–126 cm; males 730–990 g, females 970–1,300 g
animal.behaviour: Hunts by fast, contour-hugging flight, surprising mammals before they can reach their burrows.
fieldMarks: Large, brown falcon with a pale, often whitish, streaked head
Thin, faint moustache stripe
Brown upperparts with rufous edges; heavily streaked underparts
Long tail and broad-based wings; dark underwing coverts contrast with paler flight feathers
animal.voice: A harsh, scolding 'kyak-kyak-kyak' near the nest.
animal.lookalikes: Peregrine is darker slate above with a bold moustache and barred underparts. Lanner falcon (Mediterranean, Africa) is smaller with a rufous crown. Gyrfalcon (Arctic) is heavier and barred above.
animal.whereToSee: Hortobágy and Kiskunság plains (Hungary), Kazakh steppe, Mongolian steppe; on migration at Batumi and in the Middle East.
animal.season: Resident in central Europe; migratory from northern and eastern populations, wintering Oct–Mar

lore: Mongolia declared the saker its national bird in 2012, and in Hungary it is widely identified with the Turul, the mythical bird of the founding legend of the Magyars.
funFact: A Mongolian project installing thousands of artificial nests on the open steppe created a large new breeding population of sakers.

summary: The smallest of the cranes, elegant and grey with a black breast and white plumes trailing behind the eyes. Steppe populations migrate across the Himalaya and the deserts of the Middle East to winter in India and Africa.
nativeRange: Breeds on steppes from Ukraine and southern Russia through Kazakhstan and Central Asia to Mongolia and China; a few in Turkey; formerly bred in the Atlas of Morocco; winters in South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa
abilities: Flies over the Himalaya at great altitude on migration to India
Nests on dry steppe, often far from water, unlike most cranes
Gathers in wintering flocks of thousands
Pairs dance with leaps and bows like larger cranes

animal.diet: Seeds, grain, plant shoots; insects, lizards and worms
animal.habitat: Grassy and shrubby steppe and semi-desert near streams; farmland in winter
animal.behaviour: Pairs perform graceful dances, and winter flocks descend on fields with loud bugling.
fieldMarks: Small, slim blue-grey crane
Black head, neck and long, drooping breast plumes
White tufts of plumes behind the eye
Short bill; grey tail without a bushy bustle
animal.voice: A higher-pitched, more wooden trumpeting than the common crane, 'krrro-krrro'.
animal.lookalikes: Common crane is larger, with a white neck stripe, red crown and bushy tail-bustle. Grey heron flies with neck folded.
animal.whereToSee: Kalmykian and Kazakh steppes in summer; Khichan village in Rajasthan and the Indus floodplains of Pakistan in winter; passage through Pakistan and Arabia.
animal.season: Summer visitor to breeding steppes Apr–Sep; winter visitor to South Asia and Africa Oct–Mar

lore: In Punjabi, Sindhi and Rajasthani folk songs the 'koonj' is a messenger and a metaphor for a woman far from home, and the villagers of Khichan, Rajasthan, have fed wintering flocks grain for generations.
funFact: Unlike most cranes it often nests on dry ground far from water, laying its eggs among a few pebbles with almost no nest.

summary: A white wader with a long, flat bill that widens into a spoon at the tip. It feeds by sweeping the bill from side to side through shallow water, snapping it shut on anything it touches.
nativeRange: Breeds patchily from the Netherlands, Spain and the Danube across the Middle East and Central Asia to China and India; also on the Banc d'Arguin and Red Sea; winters in West Africa, the Mediterranean, Middle East and South Asia
abilities: Detects prey by touch with sensory receptors in its spatulate bill
Feeds day and night by sweeping through water and mud
Chicks hatch with straight, short bills that develop the spoon as they grow
Has recolonised Britain, breeding at Holkham, Norfolk, since 2010

animal.diet: Small fish, shrimps, aquatic insects, tadpoles and molluscs
animal.habitat: Shallow marshes, lagoons, reedbeds and estuaries
animal.behaviour: Feeding birds wade in lines, swinging their heads side to side in a sweeping arc.
fieldMarks: All-white plumage
Long black bill with a yellow spoon-shaped tip
Breeding adults have a bushy crest and yellow-ochre breast patch
Flies with neck outstretched, unlike egrets
animal.voice: Mostly silent; low grunting at colonies.
animal.lookalikes: Little egret and great white egret have pointed bills and fly with necks folded. African spoonbill (Africa) has a red face and red legs.
animal.whereToSee: Texel and the Wadden Sea (Netherlands), Doñana (Spain), the Danube Delta, Lake Kerkini (Greece), Banc d'Arguin (Mauritania), Holkham (England).
animal.season: Summer visitor in northern Europe; resident or winter visitor in the south and Middle East

lore: Spoonbills bred in England until the 17th century and are recorded in medieval accounts as 'shovelars' served at feasts; their return in the 21st century followed recovery in the Netherlands.
funFact: The Dutch population fell to roughly 150 pairs in the late 1960s and has since grown to several thousand pairs.

summary: A small, delicately patterned dove whose soft purring song was once a defining sound of European summer. It winters in the Sahel and has declined severely due to habitat loss and hunting on migration.
nativeRange: Breeds in Europe, North Africa, Turkey, the Middle East and Central Asia to western China; winters in sub-Saharan Africa south of the Sahara
abilities: One of the few European doves to make a long-distance migration across the Sahara
Lives largely on small seeds of arable weeds such as fumitory
Produces a soft, purring song rather than cooing
Satellite tracking shows western birds wintering in the Sahel from Senegal to Mali

animal.diet: Seeds of weeds and cereals
animal.habitat: Farmland with tall hedges, scrub, woodland edge and orchards
animal.behaviour: Feeds quietly on the ground and flies off fast and low with a flicking wing action.
fieldMarks: Rufous-orange back with black-centred scalloped feathers
Black-and-white striped patch on each side of the neck
Pinkish breast and blue-grey head
Dark tail with a white border, obvious in flight
animal.voice: A soft, purring, rolling 'turrr-turrr', repeated drowsily.
animal.lookalikes: Eurasian collared dove is larger and plain sandy-grey with a single black half-collar. Oriental turtle dove (Siberia, Central Asia) is larger and darker. Laughing dove (Middle East) is smaller and has a speckled breast band.
animal.whereToSee: Mediterranean farmland in Spain, Morocco and Turkey; Suffolk and Essex hedgerows in England; heavy passage over Malta and Cyprus.
animal.season: Summer visitor Apr–Sep

lore: The Song of Songs (2:12) proclaims 'the voice of the turtle is heard in our land', and in Persian and Urdu poetry the qomri or fakhta sings for the cypress tree; 'turtle' comes from Latin 'turtur', an imitation of its purr.
funFact: The UK population has fallen by over 90% since 1970, and it was listed globally as Vulnerable in 2015.

summary: A small, white vulture with a bare yellow face and a shaggy mane. It is one of the few birds that use tools, throwing stones to crack open ostrich eggs, and it migrates between Europe and Africa.
