nativeRange: Southern Europe, North Africa, the Middle East, Central Asia, the Indian subcontinent and sub-Saharan Africa; European and Central Asian birds winter in Africa and Arabia
abilities: Throws stones at ostrich eggs to break them, a famous case of bird tool use
Uses twigs to roll up wool for nest lining
Eats the faeces of livestock, possibly for carotenoids that colour its face
Migrants cross the Mediterranean at narrow points such as Gibraltar and the Bosphorus

animal.diet: Carrion, scraps, eggs, small animals, insects and dung
animal.habitat: Mountains and cliffs near open country, villages and rubbish dumps
animal.behaviour: Picks over scraps at carcasses and dumps, waiting its turn after larger vultures.
fieldMarks: Adult dirty-white with black flight feathers
Bare yellow-orange face and thin, hooked bill
Wedge-shaped white tail
Juveniles dark brown, whitening over about five years
animal.voice: Usually silent; occasional mewing and hissing.
animal.lookalikes: White stork is longer-legged with a red bill. Griffon vulture is much larger and brown. Booted eagle pale morph has a square tail and feathered head.
animal.whereToSee: Spanish sierras (Monfragüe, Picos de Europa), the Balkans, Socotra (Yemen) and Oman; migration at Gibraltar, Belen (Turkey) and Eilat.
animal.season: Summer visitor in Europe Mar–Sep; resident in Africa, Arabia and South Asia

lore: The hieroglyph for the sound 'aleph' (Gardiner G1) depicts this vulture, and the bird's habit of following people gave it the nickname 'Pharaoh's chicken'.
funFact: Jane Goodall and Hugo van Lawick first described its stone-throwing in Tanzania in 1966.

summary: A glossy black ibis with a bare red face, a ragged ruff and a curved red bill. Once widespread in Europe, the Middle East and North Africa, it survives in the wild mainly on Morocco's Atlantic coast, with reintroduced populations in Europe.
nativeRange: Wild colonies in Souss-Massa (Morocco); semi-wild colony at Birecik (Turkey); reintroduced in Austria, Germany, Italy and Spain; formerly Syria, central Europe and North Africa
abilities: Nests on cliff ledges in colonies
Probes soil for insects and small reptiles in dry grassland
Reintroduced European birds have learned a migration route by following ultralight aircraft
Formation flying saves energy, as studied in this species

animal.diet: Beetles, larvae, worms, lizards and other small animals
animal.habitat: Rocky coasts, cliffs and semi-arid steppe and farmland
animal.behaviour: Feeds in loose flocks, probing the ground with its curved bill while walking.
fieldMarks: Black plumage glossed with green and purple
Bare red face and head
Long, curved red bill
Shaggy ruff of feathers on the nape
animal.voice: A guttural 'hyoh' or 'chrup' and various croaks at the colony.
animal.lookalikes: Glossy ibis is slimmer with a feathered head and darker bill. Cormorants fly with straight bills. Southern bald ibis lives only in southern Africa.
animal.whereToSee: Souss-Massa National Park and Tamri (Morocco), Birecik (Turkey), and reintroduced birds in Austria and Tuscany.
animal.season: Resident in Morocco; reintroduced European birds migrate to Tuscany for winter

lore: The ancient Egyptian hieroglyph 'akh', meaning spirit or shining one, depicts this ibis, and in Birecik it was traditionally believed to guide pilgrims to Mecca.
funFact: Conrad Gessner described it in Switzerland in 1555, but after it vanished from Europe it was dismissed as a mythical bird until it was rediscovered in the Middle East.

summary: A small auk with a huge, colourful bill, nesting in burrows on grassy sea cliffs. It 'flies' underwater to catch small fish and brings them back crosswise in its bill.
nativeRange: North Atlantic: breeds from Brittany, Britain and Ireland to Iceland, Norway, the Faroes and Svalbard, and from Maine to Greenland; winters at sea, south to the Canaries and western Mediterranean
abilities: Carries a dozen or more fish at once, held against spines on its tongue and palate
Dives to depths of several tens of metres, propelled by its wings
Digs burrows with bill and feet in cliff-top turf
Its bill sheath fluoresces under ultraviolet light

animal.diet: Sandeels, sprats, capelin and other small fish
animal.habitat: Open sea; breeds on islands and cliffs with soft turf
animal.behaviour: Pairs reunite at the same burrow each year and greet each other by tapping bills ('billing').
fieldMarks: Black upperparts and collar, white face and underparts
Large, triangular bill striped red, yellow and blue-grey in summer
Orange legs and feet
Fast, whirring flight low over the sea
animal.voice: A low, growling 'arr-arr' from inside burrows; silent at sea.
animal.lookalikes: Razorbill and guillemots are larger with thinner bills and no coloured beak. Little auk is tiny with a stubby black bill. In winter the puffin's bill and face are duller.
animal.whereToSee: Skomer (Wales), Farne Islands and Isle of May (Britain), Látrabjarg and Westman Islands (Iceland), Runde (Norway), Machias Seal Island (Canada/USA).
animal.season: At colonies late Mar–early Aug; at sea in winter

lore: Lundy Island in the Bristol Channel takes its name from the Norse word 'lundi', puffin, and in medieval England the bird's fishy flesh was sometimes accepted as Lenten food.
funFact: The colourful outer bill plates are shed after the breeding season, leaving a smaller, duller bill in winter.

summary: A jay-sized bird of shining turquoise and chestnut that watches for insects from wires and dead trees. It is named for its tumbling, rolling display flight, and it migrates to southern Africa for the winter.
nativeRange: Breeds in southern and eastern Europe, North Africa, Turkey, the Middle East and Central Asia to western China and Kashmir; winters in eastern and southern Africa
abilities: Performs a tumbling, rolling display dive in spring
Nestlings vomit a foul-smelling orange fluid to deter predators
Nests in tree holes, banks and nest boxes, often old woodpecker holes
Migrates in loops across East Africa and Arabia

animal.diet: Large insects such as beetles and grasshoppers; lizards and small rodents
animal.habitat: Open country with old trees, steppe, farmland with scattered trees
animal.behaviour: Sits upright on a high perch and drops to the ground to seize prey.
fieldMarks: Bright turquoise head and underparts
Chestnut back
Deep violet-blue and black flight feathers flash in flight
Stout black bill
animal.voice: A harsh, crow-like 'rack-kack' and rattling 'krak-krak-krak' in display.
animal.lookalikes: Indian roller (Middle East, South Asia) has a rufous-pink breast and purple throat. Blue-cheeked bee-eater is green and slimmer. European bee-eater has a long, curved bill and tail streamers.
animal.whereToSee: Extremadura and the Ebro valley (Spain), the Crau and Camargue (France), Hungary, the Balkans, Turkey, Central Asian steppes; passage in East Africa.
animal.season: Summer visitor Apr/May–Aug

lore: Its Persian name 'sabzqaba' means 'green robe', and Linnaeus's 'garrulus' (chattering) refers to its harsh calls.
funFact: Studies in Spain showed roller chicks' orange vomit discourages predators and may warn parents of danger.

summary: Europe's largest woodpecker, crow-sized and all black with a red crown. The large oval holes it carves in old trees become homes for owls, stock doves, bats and pine martens.
nativeRange: Forests from Spain and France across Europe, Turkey and the Caucasus, through Russia and Siberia to Japan and northern China
abilities: Excavates large, oval nest holes that many other species later use
Rips into rotten stumps and trunks to reach carpenter ants
Drums loudly on resonant trunks to advertise territory
Its old holes are key nest sites for Tengmalm's owl, stock dove and goldeneye

animal.diet: Carpenter ants and wood-boring beetle larvae; some berries
animal.habitat: Mature conifer, beech and mixed forests with large old trees
animal.behaviour: Leaves large rectangular excavations at the base of ant-infested trees and stumps.
fieldMarks: All-black plumage, crow-sized
Male has a red crown from bill to nape; female only a red rear crown
Pale ivory bill and pale eye
Flies with a straight, flappy flight, not deeply undulating
animal.voice: A loud, whistling 'kree-kree-kree' in flight, a plaintive 'kleee-a' when perched; long, powerful drumming.
animal.lookalikes: Carrion crow and jackdaw lack the red crown and pale bill and do not climb trunks. Green woodpecker is green with a red cap. Grey-headed woodpecker is much smaller and green.
animal.whereToSee: Białowieża Forest (Poland/Belarus), the Bavarian Forest, Pyrenees, Alpine forests, Finnish taiga.
animal.season: Resident; drumming and calling most frequent Feb–Apr

lore: The species name 'martius' links it to Mars, the Roman god whose sacred bird was the woodpecker, and early naturalists called it the 'great black woodpecker'.
funFact: A single black woodpecker nest hole can be reused by other cavity-nesting animals for decades after the woodpecker leaves.

summary: A small, flat-headed owl with fierce yellow eyes and white 'eyebrows' that is often active by day, bobbing on fence posts and walls. It was the sacred owl of Athena and the emblem of ancient Athens.
nativeRange: Europe, North Africa, the Middle East and Central Asia to Mongolia and China; introduced to Britain in the 19th century and to New Zealand
abilities: Hunts by day as well as night, running after prey on the ground
Bobs its head and body when alarmed
Nests in tree holes, walls, rabbit burrows and nest boxes
Tolerates heat and arid conditions in desert edges

animal.diet: Beetles, earthworms, voles, mice, small birds and lizards
animal.habitat: Open farmland with old trees, orchards, stone walls, ruins, rocky semi-desert
animal.behaviour: Perches in the open on posts and rooftops in daylight, bobbing up and down when disturbed.
fieldMarks: Small, plump, round-winged owl with a flat head
Brown plumage spotted with white
Yellow eyes with white eyebrows giving a frowning look
Bounding, woodpecker-like flight
animal.voice: A plaintive, rising 'kiew' or 'goo-ek', and a sharp 'kip-kip' alarm.
animal.lookalikes: Scops owl is smaller, greyer and has ear tufts. Boreal (Tengmalm's) owl has a pale facial disc with dark border and lives in forest. Tawny owl is much larger with dark eyes.
animal.whereToSee: Olive groves and farmland in Spain, Italy and Greece; Dutch and Belgian pollard willows; farmland in central England; ruins in the Middle East.
animal.season: Resident

lore: The owl on Athenian silver tetradrachms from the 5th century BC is a little owl, giving rise to the proverb 'bringing owls to Athens', and a modern Greek one-euro coin still carries the design.
funFact: Little owls were introduced to England from the Netherlands by Victorian landowners such as Lord Lilford in the late 19th century.

summary: A dark, powerful eagle with brilliant white shoulder patches, found only in the Iberian Peninsula. Rescued from near-extinction in the 1970s, it has become one of Europe's great conservation recoveries, though it remains Vulnerable.
nativeRange: Endemic to the Iberian Peninsula (central and southwestern Spain, southern Portugal); has occasionally bred in Morocco
abilities: Specialises on rabbits, and its breeding success tracks rabbit numbers
Builds large stick nests in cork oaks and pines
Adults hold territories year-round
Young birds wander widely across Iberia before settling

animal.diet: Mainly European rabbits; also hares, partridges, pigeons, ducks and carrion
animal.habitat: Open oak woodland (dehesa), Mediterranean scrub, pine forest near marshes
animal.behaviour: Pairs soar together over their territory with undulating display flights in late winter.
fieldMarks: Very dark brown body with a pale golden-buff crown and nape
Bold white patches on the shoulders and the leading edge of the wing
Grey tail with a broad dark terminal band
Juveniles pale tawny-buff with dark flight feathers
animal.voice: A deep, barking 'owk-owk-owk'.
animal.lookalikes: Eastern imperial eagle (eastern Europe, Central Asia) has smaller white shoulder patches and no white leading edge. Golden eagle has a longer tail and lacks white shoulders. Juveniles resemble young eastern imperial eagles but are unstreaked.
animal.whereToSee: Doñana National Park, Monfragüe, Sierra de Andújar and Montes de Toledo in Spain; Alentejo in Portugal.
animal.season: Resident

lore: It was named in 1861 by the German ornithologist Christian Ludwig Brehm in honour of Prince Adalbert of Bavaria, and it became a symbol of Spanish conservation through the protection of Doñana.
funFact: Electrocution on power lines and illegal poison baits were its main killers; retrofitting dangerous pylons has been central to its recovery from a few dozen pairs.

summary: A large, dark eagle that nests on the ground or on low bushes across the open steppes of Russia, Kazakhstan and Mongolia. Once common, it has crashed due to electrocution on power lines, poisoning and habitat loss.
nativeRange: Breeds from southern Russia and Kazakhstan across Central Asia to Mongolia and China; winters in East Africa, Arabia, the Middle East and South Asia
abilities: Nests on the open ground, low shrubs or pylons where no trees exist
Preys heavily on ground squirrels (sousliks)
Migrates thousands of kilometres around the Caspian and through the Middle East to Africa
Gathers in large numbers at rubbish dumps and locust swarms in winter

animal.diet: Ground squirrels, marmots, pikas, hares; carrion; termites and locusts in winter
animal.habitat: Dry steppe and semi-desert; savanna and farmland in winter
animal.behaviour: Thousands funnel through narrow migration bottlenecks, including Eilat in Israel and Bab-el-Mandeb between Yemen and Djibouti.
fieldMarks: Large, uniformly dark brown eagle
Long gape line reaching back below the eye
Juveniles show a broad white band across the underwing and pale trailing edge
Fingered wingtips; adults often have a rufous nape patch
animal.voice: Generally silent; a barking call near the nest.
animal.lookalikes: Greater spotted eagle is darker with a shorter gape and a more compact shape. Tawny eagle (Africa, India) is paler with a shorter gape. Golden eagle has a longer tail and golden nape.
animal.whereToSee: Kalmykia and Kazakh steppe in summer; spring passage at Eilat (Israel); winter in Oman's Raysut dump and East African savanna.
animal.season: Summer visitor to breeding steppes Apr–Sep; passage Feb–Apr and Sep–Nov

lore: Its scientific name records the first specimen described from Nepal by Brian Houghton Hodgson in 1833, and for decades it was lumped with the tawny eagle of Africa and India.
funFact: It was uplisted from Least Concern to Endangered in 2015 after evidence of rapid declines across its breeding range.

summary: A Critically Endangered steppe plover that breeds in Kazakhstan and southern Russia and winters in Sudan, Arabia and the Indian subcontinent. Satellite tagging revealed migration routes through Syria and Iraq where hunting kills many.
nativeRange: Breeds in the steppes of Kazakhstan and adjacent Russia; winters in Sudan, Eritrea, Saudi Arabia, Oman, Pakistan and northwestern India
abilities: Breeds in loose colonies on heavily grazed steppe, often near villages
Travels in flocks along a long overland migration route
Relies on grazing livestock to keep steppe vegetation short
Uses fallow fields and short grassland on migration

animal.diet: Beetles, grasshoppers and other insects; some seeds
animal.habitat: Dry steppe with short, grazed vegetation; arable land and semi-desert in winter
animal.behaviour: Gathers in flocks at stopover sites in autumn, feeding on fallow and stubble fields.
fieldMarks: Black crown and eye-stripe with a bold white eyebrow
Sandy-grey body; breeding adults have a black-and-chestnut belly
Black primaries, white secondaries and black tail band in flight
Long dark legs
animal.voice: A harsh, grating 'kretch-kretch-kretch', the basis of its Russian name.
animal.lookalikes: White-tailed lapwing has a plain head and an all-white tail. Northern lapwing has a long crest and dark green back. Cream-coloured courser is smaller and runs fast with a curved bill.
animal.whereToSee: Breeding colonies in the Korgalzhyn region of Kazakhstan; wintering birds in Oman, Pakistan and Gujarat/Rajasthan; passage in southeastern Turkey.
animal.season: Summer visitor to Kazakhstan Apr–Aug; winter visitor Oct–Mar

lore: Pallas described it from the Russian steppe in 1771, and its sharp call gave it the Russian name 'kretchetka'.
funFact: In 2007 satellite-tracked birds led researchers to a flock of about 3,200 sociable lapwings in southeastern Turkey, far more than anyone thought survived.

summary: A sleek, waxwing-like grey bird with a black mask, the only member of its family. It breeds in the river valleys and deserts of Iraq, Iran and Central Asia and winters in date palm oases around the Persian Gulf.
nativeRange: Breeds in Iraq, Iran, Turkmenistan and Afghanistan; winters in eastern Arabia, Bahrain, Kuwait, the UAE, southern Iran and Pakistan, with strays to western India
abilities: Sole living member of the family Hypocoliidae
Feeds largely on dates and berries in winter roosts
Gathers in communal winter roosts in dense palm groves
Breeds in tamarisk and date palm scrub in hot lowland deserts

animal.diet: Fruits including dates, mulberries and berries; some insects
animal.habitat: Date palm groves, gardens and scrub along rivers in arid lands
animal.behaviour: Small parties move together between fruiting trees, often perching hidden in dense foliage and flying out to roosts at dawn.
fieldMarks: Smooth, pale grey plumage with a long tail
Male has a black mask that joins around the nape
Black tips to the primaries and a black tail tip
Female plainer brownish-grey with no mask
animal.voice: A soft, mewing 'whee-oo' and low chattering in flocks.
animal.lookalikes: Great grey and southern grey shrikes have hooked bills and black-and-white wings. Bohemian waxwing has a crest and yellow tail tip and does not occur in the Gulf.
animal.whereToSee: Winter roosts in Bahrain, the Al-Ahsa oasis in Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and the UAE.
animal.season: Winter visitor to Arabia Nov–Mar; summer visitor to breeding grounds

lore: Charles Lucien Bonaparte described it in 1850, and its relationships puzzled ornithologists for over a century until DNA studies placed it near the silky-flycatchers and waxwings.
funFact: It is one of the few bird families found only in the Middle East and southwest Asia.

summary: The only European songbird that swims and walks underwater. This chunky, white-bibbed bird bobs on boulders in fast mountain streams before plunging in to hunt insect larvae on the riverbed.
nativeRange: Fast rivers of Europe, northwest Africa (Atlas), Turkey, the Caucasus, Iran and Central Asia to the Himalaya and western China
abilities: Walks along the stream bed against the current, using its wings to stay down
Has dense plumage and a large preen gland for waterproofing
Can close its nostrils with flaps of skin when submerged
Sings through the winter, even beside frozen torrents

animal.diet: Caddisfly, mayfly and stonefly larvae, freshwater shrimps, small fish
animal.habitat: Clear, fast-flowing upland streams and rivers
animal.behaviour: Bobs constantly on a stone in midstream, blinking its white eyelids, before diving in.
fieldMarks: Plump, short-tailed, wren-like shape
Bright white throat and breast
Dark chocolate-brown head and blackish body; some races have a chestnut belly band
Whirring, low flight over water
animal.voice: A sharp, metallic 'zit' in flight; song a sweet, rambling warble heard even in winter.
animal.lookalikes: Ring ouzel has a white breast crescent but is a thrush of moorland, not water. Brown dipper (Central Asia, Himalaya) is entirely brown with no white bib.
animal.whereToSee: Upland streams in Wales, northern England and Scotland, the Alps, Pyrenees, Norwegian rivers and Atlas Mountains.
animal.season: Resident; northern birds move to ice-free water in winter

lore: Norway made the dipper (fossekall, 'waterfall man') its national bird in 1963, and the Welsh name 'bronwen y dŵr' means 'white breast of the water'.
funFact: Studies in Wales found dipper numbers fell on acidified streams, making it an indicator of river health.

summary: A tawny, long-tailed bird of reedbeds whose males sport a black drooping 'moustache'. Despite its old name 'bearded tit', it is the only member of its own family.
nativeRange: Reedbeds patchily from Britain and Spain across Europe, Turkey and the Middle East to Central Asia, Mongolia and northeastern China
abilities: Switches diet from insects in summer to reed seeds in winter
Changes its gizzard structure seasonally and swallows grit to grind seeds
Clings to reed stems with legs straddled between two stalks
Sole member of the family Panuridae

animal.diet: Insects and spiders in summer; reed seeds in autumn and winter
animal.habitat: Extensive reedbeds by lakes, rivers and estuaries
animal.behaviour: Flocks erupt from reedbeds in autumn, flying high and calling before moving to new marshes.
fieldMarks: Tawny-orange body and very long, graduated tail
Male: blue-grey head and broad black moustache
Yellow-orange bill and eye
Whirring flight just above the reed tops
animal.voice: A ringing, metallic 'ping' or 'tching', often the first clue to its presence.
animal.lookalikes: Long-tailed tit is smaller with a pink, black and white pattern and lives in woodland. Reed warblers are brown with short tails.
animal.whereToSee: Minsmere and the Norfolk Broads (England), Oostvaardersplassen (Netherlands), the Danube Delta, Lake Neusiedl (Austria/Hungary).
animal.season: Resident; mass movements Sep–Nov

lore: The species name 'biarmicus' refers to Biarmia, an old name for the region around the White Sea, although the bird does not live there.
funFact: Severe winters can wipe out local populations, which then recover in a few years thanks to multiple broods.

summary: A tiny ball of fluff with a tail longer than its body, travelling through woodland in chattering family flocks. Its domed nest of moss, lichen and spider silk is one of the finest bird constructions in Europe.
nativeRange: Europe, Turkey, the Caucasus and northern Iran across Siberia and Central Asia to Japan and Korea
abilities: Builds a stretchy, domed nest bound with spider silk and lined with up to about 2,000 feathers
Birds whose own nest fails often help feed the chicks of relatives
Huddles in tight rows at night to survive cold
Recognises relatives by their calls

animal.diet: Small insects, spiders and their eggs; occasionally seeds
animal.habitat: Deciduous woodland, scrub, hedges and gardens
animal.size: 13–15 cm including a 7–9 cm tail; 7–9 g
animal.behaviour: Family flocks of 10–20 birds roam through trees in winter, one following another across gaps.
fieldMarks: Tiny round body with a very long black tail edged in white
Pinkish shoulders and flanks
White crown with broad black stripes in western birds; pure white head in northern caudatus
Short, stubby bill
animal.voice: A thin, high 'tsee-tsee-tsee', a dry rolling 'tsirrup' and a short 'tup' contact call.
animal.lookalikes: Bearded reedling is tawny and lives in reedbeds. Pied wagtail is larger, walks on the ground and wags its tail.
animal.whereToSee: Woodland edges, hedgerows and garden feeders throughout Europe; white-headed birds in Scandinavia and Russia.
animal.season: Resident

lore: Its bottle-shaped nest gave it old English names such as 'bottle tit' and 'feather poke', and the white-headed Hokkaido race, 'shima-enaga', has become a popular mascot in Japan.
funFact: A nest can take two to three weeks to build and expands as the chicks grow, thanks to its stretchy silk and moss construction.

summary: A secretive, streaky-brown heron of dense reedbeds, almost invisible when it freezes with its bill pointed skyward. In spring the male's booming call carries across the marshes like a distant foghorn.
nativeRange: Europe, North Africa, Turkey, the Middle East, Central Asia to Japan; southern African population; northern birds winter south to Africa and South Asia
abilities: Booming call can be heard up to several kilometres away
Freezes with neck stretched and bill up, swaying with the reeds as camouflage
Its eyes are positioned to see forward even when the bill points straight up
Booming is produced by inflating the oesophagus

animal.diet: Fish (especially eels), frogs, insects and small mammals
animal.habitat: Extensive wet reedbeds with open water
animal.behaviour: Stalks slowly through the reeds, hunting in channels and pools.
fieldMarks: Golden-brown plumage boldly streaked and barred with black
Black crown and moustache stripe
Stocky heron with thick neck and greenish-yellow legs
Broad, rounded, owl-like wings in flight
animal.voice: Male's booming 'oo-pumb', given in series at dusk and dawn in spring; flight call a harsh 'kau'.
animal.lookalikes: Juvenile night heron is smaller and spotted white. Purple heron is slimmer with a long thin neck. Little bittern is much smaller with pale wing panels.
animal.whereToSee: Minsmere, Ham Wall and Lakenheath Fen (England), Biebrza Marshes (Poland), the Danube Delta, Lake Neusiedl.
animal.season: Resident in western Europe; summer visitor further east; booms Mar–Jun

lore: Chaucer's Wife of Bath compares a sound to the bittern ('as a bitore bombleth in the myre'), and its booming gave rise to folk names such as 'butterbump' and 'bog bumper'.
funFact: Britain's booming males fell to just 11 in 1997; reedbed restoration raised them to more than 200 by the early 2020s and 283 in 2024.

summary: A wader whose breeding males grow huge, colourful ruffs and ear tufts and battle at leks. Males come in three genetically fixed types, including a rare female-mimic that sneaks matings.
nativeRange: Breeds across northern Europe and Siberia; winters in Africa, the Mediterranean, the Middle East and South Asia
abilities: Three male types: territorial 'independents', satellite males with white ruffs, and 'faeders' that look like females
The male types are controlled by a supergene formed by a chromosome inversion about 3.8 million years ago
Males are much larger than females
Huge winter flocks gather in the inland delta of the Niger and other African wetlands

animal.diet: Insects and larvae, worms; seeds and rice in winter
animal.habitat: Wet meadows, marshes and tundra; flooded fields and lake shores in winter
animal.size: Males 29–32 cm, ~180 g; females 22–26 cm, ~110 g
animal.behaviour: On the lek, males posture with ruffs spread, jumping and sparring while females (reeves) choose.
fieldMarks: Breeding males have a variable ruff and ear tufts in black, chestnut, white or mixed
Scaly upperparts with pale feather fringes outside breeding
Small head, medium bill and long orange or greenish legs
White oval patches at the sides of the tail in flight
animal.voice: Largely silent; occasional low grunts.
animal.lookalikes: Redshank has red legs and a white trailing edge to the wing. Common greenshank is grey with a long upturned bill. Juveniles can suggest buff-breasted sandpiper (a rare vagrant from America).
animal.whereToSee: Breeding in Dutch, Swedish and Norwegian meadows; passage at the Wadden Sea; winter flocks in the Senegal and Niger deltas and Indian wetlands.
animal.season: Summer visitor to the north Apr–Jul; passage migrant; winter visitor to Africa and Asia

lore: Ruffs were netted and fattened for the table in 17th–18th-century England, and the bird's name echoes the starched lace ruffs of Elizabethan dress.
funFact: The faeder males, about 1% of males, were only identified in 2006.

summary: A glossy black crow with a curved scarlet bill and red legs, tumbling acrobatically along sea cliffs and mountain gorges. It is an emblem of Cornwall, where it returned naturally in 2001.
nativeRange: Atlantic coasts of Britain, Ireland and Brittany; mountains of Iberia, the Alps, Atlas, Turkey, the Caucasus, Central Asia, the Himalaya and China; also Ethiopia
abilities: Probes short turf and dung with its curved bill for soil invertebrates
Performs acrobatic dives and rolls in updrafts along cliffs
Lives at very high altitudes in the Himalaya and Tibetan Plateau
Relies on short, grazed grassland maintained by livestock

animal.diet: Ants, beetles, leatherjackets, dung invertebrates; some grain
animal.habitat: Sea cliffs with grazed turf, mountain cliffs and gorges
animal.behaviour: Pairs and flocks play in the wind along cliffs, calling as they swoop and roll.
fieldMarks: Glossy blue-black plumage
Long, decurved red bill
Red legs
Deeply fingered, broad wings in flight
animal.voice: A loud, ringing 'chee-ow' or 'kyaa', more musical than other crows.
animal.lookalikes: Alpine chough has a short yellow bill and longer tail. Jackdaw has a grey nape and a short black bill. Carrion crow is larger with a black bill and legs.
animal.whereToSee: The Lizard (Cornwall), Pembrokeshire and Anglesey (Wales), Islay (Scotland), the Picos de Europa, Atlas Mountains and Himalaya.
animal.season: Resident

lore: Cornish legend says King Arthur's soul passed into a chough, and the bird appears on Cornwall's coat of arms; its name comes from the old jackdaw-like call 'chow'.
funFact: After choughs died out in Cornwall in 1973, a wild pair arrived on the Lizard in 2001 and bred there the following year.

summary: Europe's largest eagle, with broad, plank-like wings, a massive yellow bill and a short white tail. Persecution wiped it out across much of western Europe; reintroductions have returned it to Scotland, Ireland and England.
nativeRange: Coasts and large wetlands of Norway, the Baltic, Iceland, Scotland and eastern Europe, east through Russia, Kazakhstan and Siberia to Japan; also western Greenland; winters south to Turkey, the Middle East and China
abilities: Wingspan up to about 2.5 m, the broadest of any European eagle
Snatches fish from the surface and robs otters, ospreys and gulls of food
Builds huge nests used for decades
Recovered across the Baltic after DDT and PCBs were banned

animal.diet: Fish, waterbirds, carrion and occasionally mammals
animal.habitat: Rocky coasts, large lakes, rivers and estuaries
animal.lifespan: Often 20+ years; can exceed 25 in the wild
animal.behaviour: Often sits for hours on a shoreline perch, then glides out low over the water to snatch fish.
fieldMarks: Huge, broad, rectangular wings with deeply fingered tips
Short, wedge-shaped white tail in adults
Massive yellow bill and pale head in adults
Juveniles dark with dark bill and tail
animal.voice: A yelping 'kli-kli-kli' or 'krick-krick', often given in duet by pairs.
animal.lookalikes: Golden eagle has a longer tail, narrower wings held in a shallow V and a golden nape. Osprey is white below with long, angled wings. Pallas's fish eagle (Central Asia) has a dark tail with a white band.
animal.whereToSee: Isle of Mull and Skye (Scotland), the Isle of Wight (England), Lofoten (Norway), Danube Delta, Polish lakes, Hokkaido in winter.
animal.season: Resident in the west; northern and eastern birds move south in winter

lore: Neolithic people placed white-tailed eagle bones with human remains in the 'Tomb of the Eagles' on South Ronaldsay, Orkney, around 5,000 years ago, and the eagle's Old English name 'erne' survives in place names.
funFact: The last native British bird was shot in Shetland in 1918; reintroduction began on the Isle of Rùm in 1975 with birds from Norway.
